papers.conclusion: The paper identifies repetition bias and representation collapse as key characteristics of early-phase implicit biases in Transformer training, closely connected to the loss plateau, and suggests a 'search' over sequence tokens as a possible cause.
papers.key_findings:
During the initial loss plateau, the model often learns a partial solution, correctly predicting a subset of easier tokens while failing on more complex parts.
A strong repetition bias appears in model outputs during the plateau, quantified by repetition frequency and sequence entropy.
Internal representation collapse occurs where hidden states for different tokens become nearly parallel (high cosine similarity).
Gradual learning of the optimal attention pattern commences during the plateau and precedes the sudden loss drop; intervening on attention maps alters plateau duration and degenerate behaviors.
The phenomena of repetition bias and representation collapse are also observed in the early pre-training stages of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
future_direction: Understanding why behaviors such as representation collapse exist during early time training.
Rigorous theoretical validation of the 'search' hypothesis and how it connects to task complexity.
papers.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.

papers.title: Better Pre-Training by Reducing Representation Confusion
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to reduce two types of information confusion in pre-trained language models: confusion between distance and direction in relative position encoding, and high similarity between token representations and between head representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two techniques to reduce information confusion in pre-training: DDRP encoding decouples distance and direction in relative position encoding, and MTH objective reduces similarity between token and head representations, leading to improved performance and faster pre-training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that reducing information confusion in representation learning through DDRP and MTH improves pre-trained language models, and suggests broader applications of this principle.
papers.key_findings:
DDRP outperforms classical relative position encoding (BERT-R) and other baselines (TUPE, DEBERTA) on GLUE tasks without additional computational overhead.
MTH outperforms MLM by 0.96 average GLUE score and achieves nearly 2x pre-training speedup on BERTBASE.
DDRP reduces the number of parameters for relative position encoding from 2*rs to rs+3.
MTH reduces the average cosine self-similarity of token and head representations, leading to more discriminative representations.
DDRP exhibits a stronger directional bias in attention heads, with 92.11% of sentences showing an up-down triangle effect compared to 78.94% for BERT-R.
papers.limitation: The proposed methods induce additional computational costs: DDRP increases computational cost by about 5% compared to BERT, and MTH increases cost by about 4% compared to MLM.
future_direction: Exploring broader application scenarios for reducing information confusion in representation learning.
papers.abstract: In this work, we revisit the Transformer-based pre-trained language models and identify two different types of information confusion in position encoding and model representations, respectively. Firstly, we show that in the relative position encoding, the joint modeling about relative distances and directions brings confusion between two heterogeneous information. It may make the model unable to capture the associative semantics of the same distance and the opposite directions, which in turn affects the performance of downstream tasks. Secondly, we notice the BERT with Mask Language Modeling (MLM) pre-training objective outputs similar token representations (last hidden states of different tokens) and head representations (attention weightsof different heads), which may make the diversity of information expressed by different tokens and heads limited.Motivated by the above investigation, we propose two novel techniques to improve pre-trained language models: Decoupled Directional Relative Position (DDRP) encoding and MTH pre-training objective. DDRP decouples the relative distance features and the directional features in classical relative position encoding. MTH applies two novel auxiliary regularizers besides MLM to enlarge the dissimilarities between (a) last hidden states of different tokens, and (b) attention weights of different heads. These designs allow the model to capture different categories of information more clearly, as a way to alleviate information confusion in representation learning for better optimization.Extensive experiments and ablation studies on GLUE benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers.research_question: Can distilling the internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) of a large teacher model into a smaller student model improve knowledge distillation compared to only using output probabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes distilling internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) in addition to output probabilities for knowledge distillation, which consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation on GLUE tasks.
papers.conclusion: Internal knowledge distillation is a more effective method for compressing large models into smaller ones than standard distillation, as it preserves the teacher's internal behavior and generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge distillation (using KL-divergence on attention and cosine similarity on hidden states) consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation across four GLUE datasets.
The method effectively compresses the internal behavior of the teacher into the student, as evidenced by lower KL-divergence in attention patterns.
The performance gap between internal and standard distillation increases when training data size is smaller.
The student model trained with internal distillation tends to replicate the teacher's correct and incorrect predictions more closely than a student trained with standard distillation.
The proposed progressive (PID) and stacked (SID) internal distillation algorithms allow the student to learn internal representations layer-by-layer, with SID performing best when combined with soft-label distillation throughout training.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers.title: Decoupling the "What" and "Where" With Polar Coordinate Positional Embeddings
papers.research_question: Does decoupling content and position in positional embeddings improve model performance on tasks requiring independent matches on these factors and on length extrapolation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PoPE, a positional encoding that decouples content and position in attention, leading to improved performance on tasks requiring independent matches and superior length extrapolation compared to RoPE.
papers.conclusion: PoPE decouples content and position in positional embeddings, outperforming RoPE on various sequence modeling tasks and demonstrating strong length extrapolation capabilities without fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
PoPE solves the Indirect Indexing diagnostic task with ~95% accuracy, while RoPE fails (11%).
PoPE achieves lower perplexity than RoPE on music (JSB, MAESTRO), genomic (Human Reference Genome), and language modeling (OpenWebText) datasets.
PoPE-based Transformers show higher average accuracy on zero-shot downstream tasks (LAMBADA, BLiMP, CBT, HellaSwag, PIQA, ARC-E).
PoPE demonstrates strong zero-shot length extrapolation on PG-19, outperforming RoPE and even the fine-tuned YaRN method on sequences up to 10x longer than training.
Frequency usage analysis shows PoPE uses a broader range of frequencies, including high frequencies, compared to RoPE's sparse usage.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism in a Transformer architecture matches key to query based on both content -- the what -- and position in a sequence -- the where. We present an analysis indicating that what and where are entangled in the popular RoPE rotary position embedding. This entanglement can impair performance particularly when decisions require independent matches on these two factors. We propose an improvement to RoPE, which we call Polar Coordinate Position Embeddings or PoPE, that eliminates the what-where confound. PoPE is far superior on a diagnostic task requiring indexing solely by position or by content. On autoregressive sequence modeling in music, genomic, and natural language domains, Transformers using PoPE as the positional encoding scheme outperform baselines using RoPE with respect to evaluation loss (perplexity) and downstream task performance. On language modeling, these gains persist across model scale, from 124M to 774M parameters. Crucially, PoPE shows strong zero-shot length extrapolation capabilities compared not only to RoPE but even a method designed for extrapolation, YaRN, which requires additional fine tuning and frequency interpolation.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.research_question: Can self-supervised learning, particularly DINO-based knowledge distillation, learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images?
papers.core_contribution: Vision Transformers using DINO-based self-supervised learning learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images, with different attention heads capturing distinct morphological phenotypes.
papers.conclusion: Self-supervised learning, particularly DINO, is effective for learning representations in histopathology, and the attention heads of Vision Transformers provide interpretable visual concepts that can aid in biomarker discovery.
papers.key_findings:
ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are a strong baseline, achieving comparable performance to self-supervised methods on many tasks.
Self-supervised features, particularly from DINO, are robust and sample-efficient, performing well with less training data.
DINO outperforms SimCLR on weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks in histopathology.
DINO's attention heads learn distinct morphological visual concepts, localizing cells, stroma tissue, and fat/air pockets.
papers.limitation: Performance benefit of self-supervised learning may vary depending on organ type (only breast tissue tested) and weakly-supervised architecture (only CLAM tested).
future_direction: Assess the utility of self-supervised methods for learning representations of histopathological images from rare diseases with data paucity of slide-level and patch-level annotations.
papers.abstract: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling. To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks. Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Analyzing Transformer Dynamics as Movement through Embedding Space
papers.research_question: How do the underlying mechanics of Transformer-based language models give rise to intelligent behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space, establishing a 'Theory of Transformers' where intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the model's composition functions.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a unified framework for understanding Transformers as movement through embedding space, explaining how intelligent behaviors emerge from the organization of embedding space and the dynamics of encoding and decoding walks.
papers.key_findings:
Intelligent behaviors map to paths in Embedding Space which the Transformer random-walks through during inference.
LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths, assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors.
The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that its proximity to a token-vector reflects co-occurrence and conditioned probability.
Attention contributes a potentially redundant association-bias to the encoding walk, which aggregates features from the context via filtering and aggregation operations.
A three-way correspondence between similarity, association, and angular proximity is established in embedding space, leading to an associative organization.
papers.limitation: Experiments on concept space theory were limited to a single benchmark (Hellaswag) and a few models.
future_direction: Further investigation into the relative impact of vector similarity, position biases, filters, and decoding method across various model flavors.
papers.abstract: Transformer based language models exhibit intelligent behaviors such as understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, acquiring knowledge, reasoning, planning, reflecting and using tools. This paper explores how their underlying mechanics give rise to intelligent behaviors. Towards that end, we propose framing Transformer dynamics as movement through embedding space. Examining Transformers through this perspective reveals key insights, establishing a Theory of Transformers: 1) Intelligent behaviours map to paths in Embedding Space which, the Transformer random-walks through during inferencing. 2) LM training learns a probability distribution over all possible paths. `Intelligence' is learnt by assigning higher probabilities to paths representing intelligent behaviors. No learning can take place in-context; context only narrows the subset of paths sampled during decoding. 5) The Transformer is a self-mapping composition function, folding a context sequence into a context-vector such that it's proximity to a token-vector reflects its co-occurrence and conditioned probability. Thus, the physical arrangement of vectors in Embedding Space determines path probabilities. 6) Context vectors are composed by aggregating features of the sequence's tokens via a process we call the encoding walk. Attention contributes a - potentially redundant - association-bias to this process. 7) This process is comprised of two principal operation types: filtering (data independent) and aggregation (data dependent). This generalization unifies Transformers with other sequence models. Building upon this foundation, we formalize a popular semantic interpretation of embeddings into a ``concept-space theory'' and find some evidence of it's validity.

papers.title: Fusion Matters: Length-Aware Analysis of Positional-Encoding Fusion in Transformers
papers.research_question: Does the choice of positional-encoding fusion operator affect downstream performance? Is the effect dependent on sequence length? Can inductive bias be introduced at the fusion level to better handle long sequences?
papers.core_contribution: Positional-encoding fusion is a non-trivial design choice for long-sequence Transformers; learnable fusion mechanisms yield consistent performance improvements on long documents.
papers.conclusion: Positional-encoding fusion should be treated as an explicit design choice when building Transformers for long-context tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Fusion choice has negligible impact on short texts but produces consistent gains on long documents.
Gated fusion (Gate-Scalar) outperforms additive fusion on long documents.
The benefit of learnable fusion generalizes across multiple positional encoding families.
Local convolutional gating (Gate-CNN) introduces inductive bias but shows less stable improvements than Gate-Scalar.
Paired-seed analysis confirms the structural nature of the gains on long documents.
papers.limitation: Focuses on classification tasks and a single Transformer architecture; analysis limited to four positional encoding families.
future_direction: Extend analysis to generative tasks.
Extend analysis to hybrid encodings (e.g., ALiBi).
Extend analysis to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Transformers require positional encodings to represent sequence order, yet most prior work focuses on designing new positional encodings rather than examining how positional information is fused with token embeddings. In this paper, we study whether the fusion mechanism itself affects performance, particularly in long-sequence settings. We conduct a controlled empirical study comparing three canonical fusion strategies--element-wise addition, concatenation with projection, and scalar gated fusion--under identical Transformer architectures, data splits, and random seeds. Experiments on three text classification datasets spanning short (AG News), medium (IMDB), and long (ArXiv) sequences show that fusion choice has negligible impact on short texts but produces consistent gains on long documents. To verify that these gains are structural rather than stochastic, we perform paired-seed analysis and cross-dataset comparison across sequence-length regimes. Additional experiments on the ArXiv dataset indicate that the benefit of learnable fusion generalizes across multiple positional encoding families. Finally, we explore a lightweight convolutional gating mechanism that introduces local inductive bias at the fusion level, evaluated on long documents only. Our results indicate that positional-encoding fusion is a non-trivial design choice for long-sequence Transformers and should be treated as an explicit modeling decision rather than a fixed default.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength. We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Computation Mechanism Behind LLM Position Generalization
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) computationally process positional information to enable position generalization, such as tolerance to position perturbations and length generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that LLMs learn a disentanglement of attention logits into positional and semantic components, with a linear correlation of 0.959, and identifies a pattern in intermediate features that enables this effect, providing computational explanations for position generalization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention logits in LLMs can be approximately disentangled into independent positional and semantic components, providing computational explanations for position generalization and insights for controlling these phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Attention logits can be approximated by a 3-axis linear decomposition with high correlation.
Attention logits can be disentangled into a sum of positional relevance and semantic importance components.
A pattern in slow-rotating dimensions of query and key vectors enables this disentanglement, which is learned rather than inherent.
LLMs exhibit robustness to position perturbations in text, feature order, and position encoding, with minimal impact on perplexity and downstream task accuracy.
The disentanglement mechanism explains how length generalization techniques work by keeping attention outputs in-distribution.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily evaluates position robustness involving text order and length generalizations, but real-world language processing tasks often involve more complex positional dependencies.
The extent to which models actively leverage this property during training is unclear.
future_direction: Future research could delve deeper into the specific architectural choices and training data patterns that contribute to this robustness.
Future explanations on how such a mechanism is acquired during training dynamics could greatly enhance the work.
papers.abstract: Most written natural languages are composed of sequences of words and sentences. Similar to humans, large language models (LLMs) exhibit flexibility in handling textual positions - a phenomenon we term position generalization. They can understand texts with position perturbations and generalize to longer texts than those encountered during training with the latest techniques. These phenomena suggest that LLMs handle positions tolerantly, but how LLMs computationally process positional relevance remains largely unexplored. This work connects the linguistic phenomenon with LLMs' computational mechanisms. We show how LLMs enforce certain computational mechanisms for the aforementioned tolerance in position perturbations. Despite the complex design of the self-attention mechanism, this work reveals that LLMs learn a counterintuitive disentanglement of attention logits. Their values show a 0.959 linear correlation with an approximation of the arithmetic sum of positional relevance and semantic importance. Furthermore, we identify a prevalent pattern in intermediate features, which we prove theoretically enables this effect. The pattern, which is different from how randomly initialized parameters would behave, suggests that it is a learned behavior rather than a natural result of the model architecture. Based on these findings, we provide computational explanations and criteria for LLMs' position flexibilities. This work takes a pioneering step in linking position generalization with modern LLMs' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: On the Computational Power of Transformers and Its Implications in Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: What is the computational power of Transformers as captured by Turing-completeness, and which components are necessary for this power?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides alternate proofs that vanilla Transformers and directional Transformers (with positional masking only) are Turing-complete, and analyzes the necessity of various components for this completeness.
papers.conclusion: The class of languages recognized by Transformers and RNNs are exactly the same, implying that differences in performance arise from learning abilities rather than computational power.
papers.key_findings:
Vanilla Transformers are Turing-complete.
Directional Transformers (with positional masking and no explicit positional encodings) are also Turing-complete.
The decoder-encoder attention block is necessary for Turing-completeness.
The residual connection around the decoder-encoder attention block is necessary for Turing-completeness.
The feedforward network in the decoder is necessary for Turing-completeness.
papers.limitation: The proofs rely on arbitrary precision, which is not practical as implementations use fixed precision.
future_direction: Study of Transformers in finite precision settings.
papers.abstract: Transformers are being used extensively across several sequence modeling tasks. Significant research effort has been devoted to experimentally probe the inner workings of Transformers. However, our conceptual and theoretical understanding of their power and inherent limitations is still nascent. In particular, the roles of various components in Transformers such as positional encodings, attention heads, residual connections, and feedforward networks, are not clear. In this paper, we take a step towards answering these questions. We analyze the computational power as captured by Turing-completeness. We first provide an alternate and simpler proof to show that vanilla Transformers are Turing-complete and then we prove that Transformers with only positional masking and without any positional encoding are also Turing-complete. We further analyze the necessity of each component for the Turing-completeness of the network; interestingly, we find that a particular type of residual connection is necessary. We demonstrate the practical implications of our results via experiments on machine translation and synthetic tasks.

papers.title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning: Modality Asymmetries and Circuit Dynamics in modern Transformers
papers.research_question: What enables transformers to perform multimodal ICL, both in terms of training data statistics and mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a learning asymmetry in multimodal ICL where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers a learning asymmetry where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE increases the data complexity threshold for ICL emergence.
Multimodal ICL exhibits a learning asymmetry: with high-diversity primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices.
Scaling up unimodal models favors in-weight memorization over ICL, but scaling improves multimodal ICL.
Multimodal ICL relies on induction-style mechanisms that copy labels from matching in-context exemplars.
Encoders improve multimodal ICL by aligning features and providing discriminative representations.
papers.limitation: Observations on production MLLMs are not intended as a mechanistic explanation due to vastly more complex training regimes, data distributions, and architectural choices that confound clean attribution.
future_direction: Investigate circuit-level robustness.
Explore architectural designs that inherently favor robust reasoning over memorization.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based multimodal large language models often exhibit in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Motivated by this phenomenon, we ask: how do transformers learn to associate information across modalities from in-context examples? We investigate this question through controlled experiments on small transformers trained on synthetic classification tasks, enabling precise manipulation of data statistics and model architecture. We begin by revisiting core principles of unimodal ICL in modern transformers. While several prior findings replicate, we find that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) increases the data complexity threshold for ICL. Extending to the multimodal setting reveals a fundamental learning asymmetry: when pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices for multimodal ICL to emerge. Mechanistic analysis shows that both settings rely on an induction-style mechanism that copies labels from matching in-context exemplars; multimodal training refines and extends these circuits across modalities. Our findings provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding multimodal ICL in modern transformers and introduce a controlled testbed for future investigation.

papers.title: Positional Attention: Expressivity and Learnability of Algorithmic Computation
papers.research_question: How can Transformers execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings? What are the expressivity and learnability properties of such positional Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces positional attention, a variant where attention weights depend only on positional encodings, and shows that positional Transformers are as expressive as parallel computational models with logarithmic depth overhead, have favorable generalization bounds, and exhibit better out-of-distribution generalization on tasks relying on positional information.
papers.conclusion: Positional attention decouples attention from input values, maintaining expressivity while offering better theoretical norm dependence and improved out-of-distribution generalization for tasks that rely on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Positional Transformers can simulate the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model with O(log n) layers, where n is the input length.
Positional Transformers have norm-based generalization bounds that remove exponential dependence on depth compared to standard Transformers, implying they can learn algorithmic tasks via empirical risk minimization.
Empirically, positional Transformers show better out-of-distribution generalization than standard Transformers on tasks where the underlying algorithmic solution relies solely on positional information.
For tasks requiring dynamic communication patterns (e.g., induction heads), positional Transformers perform poorly, likely due to the difficulty of discovering good parameters during training.
There is a trade-off: positional Transformers may require more layers for certain tasks, which can increase sample complexity despite better dependence on parameter norms.
papers.limitation:
Simulation of standard Transformers by positional Transformers incurs an additional quadratic dependency on the number of nodes.
Positional Transformers perform poorly on tasks requiring dynamic communication, such as induction heads.
Positional Transformers may require more layers for certain tasks, potentially increasing sample complexity.
future_direction: In-depth work within the mechanistic interpretability framework to analyze training dynamics and reasons for failure in standard Transformers.
Theoretical analysis of out-of-distribution generalization bounds for deep positional attention architectures, considering training dynamics.
Exploring the exact causes and difficulty of achieving goals like ignoring input values and preserving positional encodings in standard Transformers.
papers.abstract: There is a growing interest in the ability of neural networks to execute algorithmic tasks (e.g., arithmetic, summary statistics, and sorting). The goal of this work is to better understand the role of attention in Transformers for algorithmic execution. Its importance for algorithmic execution has been studied theoretically and empirically using parallel computational models. Notably, many parallel algorithms communicate between processors solely using positional information. Inspired by this observation, we investigate how Transformers can execute algorithms using positional attention, where attention weights depend exclusively on positional encodings. We prove that Transformers with positional attention (positional Transformers) maintain the same expressivity of parallel computational models, incurring a logarithmic depth cost relative to the input length. We analyze their in-distribution learnability and explore how parameter norms in positional attention affect sample complexity. Our results show that positional Transformers introduce a learning trade-off: while they exhibit better theoretical dependence on parameter norms, certain tasks may require more layers, which can, in turn, increase sample complexity. Finally, we empirically explore the out-of-distribution performance of positional Transformers and find that they perform well in tasks where their underlying algorithmic solution relies on positional information.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task
papers.research_question: Does a sequence model trained on a synthetic task (Othello game transcripts) learn an internal representation of the board state, and is that representation causal to its predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that a GPT model trained on Othello game transcripts learns a nonlinear internal representation of the board state, which is causally involved in its predictions. It introduces intervention techniques and latent saliency maps for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The experiments provide evidence that Othello-GPT maintains a nonlinear internal representation of the game board state, which is causally linked to its predictions. The tools introduced (nonlinear probes, interventions, latent saliency maps) may prove useful for interpretability in natural language settings.
papers.key_findings:
Othello-GPT predicts legal moves with high accuracy, and this is not due to memorization.
Nonlinear probes can accurately decode the board state from internal activations, while linear probes perform poorly.
Intervention experiments show that the board representation is causal to the model's predictions.
Latent saliency maps reveal differences between models trained on synthetic vs. championship data, indicating different learned strategies.
The internal representation of the board state is nonlinear and emerges during training.
papers.limitation: Latent saliency maps only attribute to one tile when multiple tiles are involved in a move, which does not fully capture the Othello rule logic.
future_direction: Extend investigation to other, more complex games.
Compare strategies learned by a sequence model with those of a model trained with a priori knowledge of Othello.
Study how results generalize to natural language models.
papers.abstract: Language models show a surprising range of capabilities, but the source of their apparent competence is unclear. Do these networks just memorize a collection of surface statistics, or do they rely on internal representations of the process that generates the sequences they see? We investigate this question by applying a variant of the GPT model to the task of predicting legal moves in a simple board game, Othello. Although the network has no a priori knowledge of the game or its rules, we uncover evidence of an emergent nonlinear internal representation of the board state. Interventional experiments indicate this representation can be used to control the output of the network and create "latent saliency maps" that can help explain predictions in human terms.

papers.title: The Stem Cell Hypothesis: Dilemma behind Multi-Task Learning with Transformer Encoders
papers.research_question: Why does multi-task learning (MTL) with transformer encoders on distinct core NLP tasks lead to worse performance than single-task learning, and is there a subset of attention heads that are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for all?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the Stem Cell Hypothesis, which states that a subset of attention heads (stem cells) are naturally talented for many tasks but cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks, leading to interference and worse performance in multi-task learning.
papers.conclusion: The Stem Cell Hypothesis sheds light on the dilemma of multi-task learning with transformer encoders, indicating that attention heads cannot be jointly trained for multiple distinct tasks without interference, and suggests a direction for future MTL research by wisely assigning heads to tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-task learning on five core NLP tasks (POS, NER, DEP, CON, SRL) results in lower performance than single-task learning for all tasks.
Pruning analysis reveals that all five tasks rely on a similar set of attention heads, primarily in middle layers (5-8), which are termed 'stem cells'.
Even without fine-tuning, certain attention heads (stem cells) show high probing accuracy for specific linguistic labels, demonstrating their pluripotency.
During single-task learning, stem cells become specialized for the task, but during multi-task learning, they lose specialization due to conflicting training signals.
The Stem Cell Hypothesis is validated by novel parameter-free probes that show how attention heads are transformed during training, with MTL often degrading probing and task performance.
future_direction: Adapt the work to more tasks and languages for broader generality.
Design another probing method for deeper analysis in constituency parsing (CON).
papers.abstract: Multi-task learning with transformer encoders (MTL) has emerged as a powerful technique to improve performance on closely-related tasks for both accuracy and efficiency while a question still remains whether or not it would perform as well on tasks that are distinct in nature. We first present MTL results on five NLP tasks, POS, NER, DEP, CON, and SRL, and depict its deficiency over single-task learning. We then conduct an extensive pruning analysis to show that a certain set of attention heads get claimed by most tasks during MTL, who interfere with one another to fine-tune those heads for their own objectives. Based on this finding, we propose the Stem Cell Hypothesis to reveal the existence of attention heads naturally talented for many tasks that cannot be jointly trained to create adequate embeddings for all of those tasks. Finally, we design novel parameter-free probes to justify our hypothesis and demonstrate how attention heads are transformed across the five tasks during MTL through label analysis. papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: What Can Transformer Learn with Varying Depth? Case Studies on Sequence Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the minimum number of attention layers required for transformers to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization tasks, and what are the roles of different layers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a single-layer transformer can memorize but fails at reasoning and generalization; two layers are needed for reasoning and generalization, and three layers may be needed for contextual generalization. It also identifies simple operations that single attention layers can perform and how stacking layers combines them.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that depth is crucial for transformers to perform complex tasks, and their analysis sheds light on how transformers work by combining simple operations.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer transformer can memorize sequences but cannot perform reasoning or generalization tasks.
A two-layer transformer can perform reasoning and generalization tasks.
A three-layer transformer may be needed for contextual generalization.
Single attention layers can perform copying, parsing, matching, and mapping operations; stacking layers combines these to solve complex tasks.
Theoretical proofs and numerical experiments support these findings.
papers.abstract: We study the capabilities of the transformer architecture with varying depth. Specifically, we designed a novel set of sequence learning tasks to systematically evaluate and comprehend how the depth of transformer affects its ability to perform memorization, reasoning, generalization, and contextual generalization. We show a transformer with only one attention layer can excel in memorization but falls short in other tasks. Then, we show that exhibiting reasoning and generalization ability requires the transformer to have at least two attention layers, while context generalization ability may necessitate three attention layers. Additionally, we identify a class of simple operations that a single attention layer can execute, and show that the complex tasks can be approached as the combinations of these simple operations and thus can be resolved by stacking multiple attention layers. This sheds light on studying more practical and complex tasks beyond our design. Numerical experiments corroborate our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and why does knowledge distillation outperform learning from raw data? The paper investigates this by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method to interpret knowledge distillation by quantifying visual concepts encoded in intermediate layers of DNNs, and proposes and verifies three hypotheses explaining why knowledge distillation leads to better performance than learning from raw data.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge distillation ensures DNNs learn more task-relevant concepts, have a higher learning speed (simultaneous concept learning), and optimize with less detours than learning from raw data, as verified by the proposed quantification metrics.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more task-relevant visual concepts and fewer task-irrelevant concepts than learning from raw data.
Knowledge distillation ensures the DNN learns various visual concepts simultaneously, whereas learning from raw data tends to learn concepts sequentially.
Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions (fewer 'detours') than learning from raw data.
The proposed entropy-based metrics can quantify and compare visual concepts across different layers and network architectures.
Experiments on multiple DNN architectures and datasets generally support the three hypotheses.
papers.limitation:
The work only focuses on the classification task; applying the methods to other tasks (e.g., object segmentation) or data types (e.g., video) is theoretically feasible but not explored.
The learning procedure of DNNs cannot be precisely divided into a learning phase and a discarding phase; the target epoch for measuring concept richness is a rough estimation.
future_direction: Applying the proposed methods to other tasks such as object segmentation.
Applying the proposed methods to other types of data such as video.
papers.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers.title: Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design or: How I learned to start worrying about prompt formatting
papers.research_question: How sensitive are large language models to subtle, meaning-preserving changes in prompt formatting?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs are extremely sensitive to semantically equivalent prompt formatting choices, and introduces FORMAT SPREAD, a method to efficiently estimate the performance spread across plausible formats without accessing model weights.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that research evaluating LLMs with prompting should report performance across a range of plausible prompt formats rather than a single format, and that FORMAT SPREAD facilitates this systematic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs show extreme sensitivity to prompt formatting, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points between equivalent formats.
Sensitivity persists even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or with instruction tuning.
Format performance only weakly correlates between models, questioning the validity of comparing models with a single, fixed prompt format.
Small atomic changes in format (e.g., casing, separators) can lead to large, unpredictable accuracy changes.
Prompt formats are highly identifiable from the model's internal representations (prompt embeddings), and this identifiability correlates with performance spread.
papers.limitation: Some generated prompt formats may be unnatural (e.g., due to parsing choices or unusual separators), and the study is limited to tasks with reasonably short input instructions and field length.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are adopted as a fundamental component of language technologies, it is crucial to accurately characterize their performance. Because choices in prompt design can strongly influence model behavior, this design process is critical in effectively using any modern pre-trained generative language model. In this work, we focus on LLM sensitivity to a quintessential class of meaning-preserving design choices: prompt formatting. We find that several widely used open-source LLMs are extremely sensitive to subtle changes in prompt formatting in few-shot settings, with performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points when evaluated using LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity remains even when increasing model size, the number of few-shot examples, or performing instruction tuning. Our analysis suggests that work evaluating LLMs with prompting-based methods would benefit from reporting a range of performance across plausible prompt formats, instead of the currently-standard practice of reporting performance on a single format. We also show that format performance only weakly correlates between models, which puts into question the methodological validity of comparing models with an arbitrarily chosen, fixed prompt format. To facilitate systematic analysis we propose FormatSpread, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates a sampled set of plausible prompt formats for a given task, and reports the interval of expected performance without accessing model weights. Furthermore, we present a suite of analyses that characterize the nature of this sensitivity, including exploring the influence of particular atomic perturbations and the internal representation of particular formats.

papers.title: Large language models implicitly learn to straighten neural sentence trajectories to construct a predictive representation of natural language
papers.research_question: How does a predictive objective (next-word prediction) shape the internal representations of autoregressive transformer models? Specifically, does the neural trajectory of a sentence become progressively straighter across network layers to facilitate prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive language models implicitly straighten the neural trajectories of sentences in their internal representations to facilitate next-word prediction via linear extrapolation, and the degree of straightening scales with model performance.
papers.conclusion: The results support the trajectory straightening hypothesis as a representational mechanism by which autoregressive transformer models construct a predictive representation of language to perform next-word prediction.
papers.key_findings:
In trained models, the curvature of sentence neural trajectories progressively decreases from the first to the middle layers.
Larger models and models trained on larger datasets exhibit greater decreases in curvature, suggesting straightening underlies better language modeling performance.
Model-generated sentences have lower curvature than human-generated ground-truth sentences from the same prompt, indicating models favor straighter trajectories for prediction.
A positive correlation exists between average sentence curvature and average sentence surprisal in the middle layers of trained models.
Untrained models do not exhibit these curvature reduction or correlation patterns.
papers.limitation:
The results are compatible with two possibilities: that prediction intrinsically favors linear state dynamics, or that it indirectly favors slower dynamics due to long predictive contexts in language. These possibilities are not distinguished.
The effects of other training objectives or fine-tuning for downstream tasks on sentence curvature have not been evaluated.
The hypothesis has not been causally tested (e.g., by ablating the model to affect only curvature and observing changes in next-word prediction behavior).
future_direction: Evaluate representation straightening in human behavioral or neural responses to language.
Test the generality of the straightening mechanism in other biological and artificial systems with a core prediction objective.
Explicitly define model objectives to build predictive representations over internal states rather than outputs.
papers.abstract: Predicting upcoming events is critical to our ability to interact with our environment. Transformer models, trained on next-word prediction, appear to construct representations of linguistic input that can support diverse downstream tasks. But how does a predictive objective shape such representations? Inspired by recent work in vision (Henaff et al., 2019), we test a hypothesis about predictive representations of autoregressive transformers. In particular, we test whether the neural trajectory of a sentence becomes progressively straighter as it passes through the network layers. The key insight is that straighter trajectories should facilitate prediction via linear extrapolation. We quantify straightness using a 1-dimensional curvature metric, and present four findings in support of the trajectory straightening hypothesis: i) In trained models, the curvature decreases from the early to the deeper layers of the network. ii) Models that perform better on the next-word prediction objective exhibit greater decreases in curvature, suggesting that this improved ability to straighten sentence trajectories may be the driver of better language modeling performance. iii) Given the same linguistic context, the sequences that are generated by the model have lower curvature than the actual continuations observed in a language corpus, suggesting that the model favors straighter trajectories for making predictions. iv) A consistent relationship holds between the average curvature and the average surprisal of sentences in the deep model layers, such that sentences with straighter trajectories also have lower surprisal. Importantly, untrained models do not exhibit these behaviors. In tandem, these results support the trajectory straightening hypothesis and provide a possible mechanism for how the geometry of the internal representations of autoregressive models supports next word prediction.

papers.title: The Double Helix inside the NLP Transformer
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer process different types of information (positional, syntactic, semantic, contextual) and is the standard method of adding positional encoding to semantic embedding optimal?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a Linear-and-Add method for combining positional encoding with semantic embedding, which outperforms simple addition, and reveals that the Transformer automatically separates positional information into a helical structure in the embedding space while conceptual dimensions form part-of-speech clusters.
papers.conclusion: The Transformer processes information at four levels (positional, syntactic, semantic, contextual) and internally separates positional information into a helical structure, while the proposed Linear-and-Add method improves performance, making the model's workings more interpretable.
papers.key_findings:
