The standard practice of adding positional encoding vectors directly to semantic embedding vectors is suboptimal; a weighted sum (optimal weight 0.3) or a Linear-and-Add approach (dense layer followed by addition) yields better performance.
After the encoding stage, the residual positional information collapses to a three-dimensional helical structure, leaving the remaining dimensions for conceptual (syntactic, semantic, contextual) information.
A second helical structure is found in the decoder's second attention layer.
Part-of-speech clusters (nouns, adjectives, verbs, and functional 'adjuvant' words) emerge in the conceptual dimensions after encoding, and self-attention layers improve this clustering.
The Transformer's architecture inherently achieves shift invariance by separating positional and conceptual dimensions, with positional encoding following a hypertorus (helix) topology.
papers.limitation: Further analysis on multiple consecutive tokens is necessary to fully understand syntactic and contextual information, which is deferred to future work.
future_direction: Further analysis on multiple consecutive tokens to understand syntactic and contextual information.
Exploring different approaches to merging positional and semantic information.
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework for analyzing various types of information in an NLP Transformer. In this approach, we distinguish four layers of information: positional, syntactic, semantic, and contextual. We also argue that the common practice of adding positional information to semantic embedding is sub-optimal and propose instead a Linear-and-Add approach. Our analysis reveals an autogenetic separation of positional information through the deep layers. We show that the distilled positional components of the embedding vectors follow the path of a helix, both on the encoder side and on the decoder side. We additionally show that on the encoder side, the conceptual dimensions generate Part-of-Speech (PoS) clusters. On the decoder side, we show that a di-gram approach helps to reveal the PoS clusters of the next token. Our approach paves a way to elucidate the processing of information through the deep layers of an NLP Transformer.

papers.title: Causality-Induced Positional Encoding for Transformer-Based Representation Learning of Non-Sequential Features
papers.research_question: How can transformer architectures be extended to data with non-sequential yet causally-related features by generating positional encodings that capture underlying causal structure without predefined feature order?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CAPE, a method to generate causality-aware positional encodings for transformers on non-sequential yet causally-related features, eliminating the need for predefined order and incorporating causal structure via hyperbolic embedding of learned causal graphs.
papers.conclusion: CAPE successfully extends transformer-based representation learning to non-sequential data by incorporating causal structure into positional encodings, with theoretical guarantees and empirical improvements across multiple omics domains.
papers.key_findings:
CAPE effectively identifies underlying causal structure and preserves it in hyperbolic embeddings, encoding causal strength as pairwise distance and causal specificity as distance to origin.
CAPE-generated rotary positional encodings exhibit causal distance-induced attention attenuation and causal generality-induced attention attenuation, as theoretically proven.
CAPE enhances transformer performance on real-world multi-omics tasks including gene perturbation prediction, cell type annotation, cell clustering, and age prediction.
The attention scores computed with CAPE are robust to positional disturbances caused by measurement errors, as shown theoretically and empirically.
Ablation studies show the importance of hyperparameters like DAG pruning threshold, k-hop neighborhood size, and causal generality regularization weight.
papers.limitation:
Effectiveness relies on the quality of the inferred causal graph, which may be inaccurate in extremely noisy or undersampled settings.
Assumes feature-wise causal structure is static across samples, which may not capture sample-specific heterogeneity in highly dynamic systems.
future_direction: Incorporating uncertainty-aware causal discovery.
Adapting CAPE to sample-dependent causal structures.
papers.abstract: Positional encoding is essential for supplementing transformer with positional information of tokens. Existing positional encoding methods demand predefined token/feature order, rendering them unsuitable for real-world data with non-sequential yet causally-related features. To address this limitation, we propose CAPE, a novel method that identifies underlying causal structure over non-sequential features as a weighted directed acyclic graph (DAG) using generalized structural equation modeling. The DAG is then embedded in hyperbolic space where its geometric structure is well-preserved using a hyperboloid model-based approach that effectively captures two important causal graph properties (causal strength & causal specificity). This step yields causality-aware positional encodings for the features, which are converted into their rotary form for integrating with transformer's self-attention mechanism. Theoretical analysis reveals that CAPE-generated rotary positional encodings possess three valuable properties for enhanced self-attention, including causal distance-induced attenuation, causal generality-induced attenuation, and robustness to positional disturbances. We evaluate CAPE over both synthetic and real-word datasets, empirically demonstrating its theoretical properties and effectiveness in enhancing transformer for data with non-sequential features. Our code is available at https://github.com/Catchxu/CAPE.

papers.title: Alternative positional encoding functions for neural transformers
papers.research_question: Can alternative periodic functions (triangular, square, sawtooth) be used for positional encoding in neural transformers, and how do they compare to the standard sinusoidal functions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes three alternative periodic functions (triangular, square, sawtooth) for positional encoding in transformers and demonstrates that they outperform the standard sinusoidal function on a machine translation benchmark.
papers.conclusion: The proposed alternative positional encoding functions clearly surpass the original sinusoidal approach, opening the path for more successful applications and potential performance enhancements and energy savings.
papers.key_findings:
All three alternative positional encoding functions (triangular, square, sawtooth) outperform the standard sinusoidal function in terms of cross-entropy loss and BLEU-4 score on the Multi30K translation task.
The triangular and sawtooth functions achieve the best performance, with the triangular function learning faster than the sawtooth function.
The square wave function, which quantizes input values, also outperforms the sinusoidal function but to a lesser extent than the triangular and sawtooth functions.
papers.limitation: Evaluation is limited to a single benchmark task (translation on Multi30K dataset) and model architecture, so generalizability to other tasks and models is not yet established.
future_direction: More experimentation with a wider range of problems to further validate the preliminary results.
Consideration of other alternative periodic functions.
papers.abstract: A key module in neural transformer-based deep architectures is positional encoding. This module enables a suitable way to encode positional information as input for transformer neural layers. This success has been rooted in the use of sinusoidal functions of various frequencies, in order to capture recurrent patterns of differing typical periods. In this work, an alternative set of periodic functions is proposed for positional encoding. These functions preserve some key properties of sinusoidal ones, while they depart from them in fundamental ways. Some tentative experiments are reported, where the original sinusoidal version is substantially outperformed. This strongly suggests that the alternative functions may have a wider use in other transformer architectures.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Relative Positional Encoding for Transformers with Linear Complexity
papers.research_question: How to incorporate relative positional encoding into linear-complexity Transformers to improve performance on long sequences?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Stochastic Positional Encoding (SPE) as a way to achieve relative positional encoding in linear-complexity Transformers, enabling them to handle long sequences effectively without computing the full attention matrix.
papers.conclusion: SPE is an effective method for incorporating relative positional information into linear Transformers, with benefits for long-sequence tasks like music generation and potential for further improvements.
papers.key_findings:
SPE allows linear-complexity Transformers to use relative positional encoding without explicit computation of the attention matrix.
SPE improves validation loss and extrapolation ability in music generation tasks, outperforming absolute positional encoding.
In the Long-Range Arena, sineSPE performs competitively, especially on the Retrieval task, but results are mixed across tasks.
SPE can be implemented with two variants: sineSPE (periodic) and convSPE (vanishing), offering flexibility for different applications.
Gated SPE allows the model to switch off positional encoding in some attention heads, which can be beneficial.
papers.limitation:
The variance of the Monte Carlo estimator in SPE might affect performance in large dimensions.
The Long-Range Arena tasks might not strongly benefit from relative positional encoding, so the advantages of SPE are not always clear.
future_direction: Exploring variance-reduced estimation methods for SPE.
Designing new long-range tasks where positional encoding is critical.
Extending SPE to arbitrary attention kernels beyond dot-product attention.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Transformer models allow for unprecedented sequence lengths, due to linear space and time complexity. In the meantime, relative positional encoding (RPE) was proposed as beneficial for classical Transformers and consists in exploiting lags instead of absolute positions for inference. Still, RPE is not available for the recent linear-variants of the Transformer, because it requires the explicit computation of the attention matrix, which is precisely what is avoided by such methods. In this paper, we bridge this gap and present Stochastic Positional Encoding as a way to generate PE that can be used as a replacement to the classical additive (sinusoidal) PE and provably behaves like RPE. The main theoretical contribution is to make a connection between positional encoding and cross-covariance structures of correlated Gaussian processes. We illustrate the performance of our approach on the Long-Range Arena benchmark and on music generation.

papers.title: Roles and Utilization of Attention Heads in Transformer-based Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are basic linguistic properties captured with the attention heads across transformer-based models and used for downstream tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an analysis method to understand where linguistic properties are learned and represented in attention heads of transformer architectures, and shows that selecting and concatenating influential attention heads can improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that understanding the roles of attention heads can lead to adaptive sentence representations that improve downstream task performance, and reveals internal behaviors of transformer models during fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads on different layers are specialized for different linguistic properties (syntactic, semantic, surface).
The last layer of transformer encoders is not always the best for representing linguistic properties; earlier layers often dominate.
Concatenating the outputs of the top-n influential attention heads (selected via probing) yields better sentence representations and improves downstream task performance.
During fine-tuning, the initial superior attention heads remain influential and their performance is amplified, while adjacent heads also show increased performance.
Attention heads handle both syntactic and semantic information in a balanced way, with a linear relationship between their syntactic and semantic scores.
future_direction: Investigation of how heat maps vary during extensive pre-training to understand the dynamics of the learning processes.
papers.abstract: Sentence encoders based on the transformer architecture have shown promising results on various natural language tasks. The main impetus lies in the pre-trained neural language models that capture long-range dependencies among words, owing to multi-head attention that is unique in the architecture. However, little is known for how linguistic properties are processed, represented, and utilized for downstream tasks among hundreds of attention heads inside the pre-trained transformerbased model. For the initial goal of examining the roles of attention heads in handling a set of linguistic features, we conducted a set of experiments with ten probing tasks and three downstream tasks on four pre-trained transformer families (GPT, GPT2, BERT, and ELECTRA). Meaningful insights are shown through the lens of heat map visualization and utilized to propose a relatively simple sentence representation method that takes advantage of most influential attention heads, resulting in additional performance improvements on the downstream tasks.

papers.title: Improving Transformers using Faithful Positional Encoding
papers.research_question: How can positional encoding in Transformers be improved by introducing a notion of faithfulness and deriving a new encoding based on discrete Fourier transform (DFT)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new positional encoding method for Transformers based on discrete Fourier transform (DFT) that is faithful (injective to the position function) and systematically improves prediction performance in time-series classification.
papers.conclusion: DFT positional encoding provides a theoretically grounded improvement over the original positional encoding and enhances performance in time-series classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The original sinusoidal positional encoding has a strong low-pass property and lacks faithfulness, meaning it loses information about positional order.
The proposed DFT encoding is faithful and provides a uniform distribution of frequencies, unlike the skewed distribution of the original encoding.
DFT encoding improves classification performance on time-series datasets, likely due to better handling of short- and mid-range dependencies.
papers.abstract: We propose a new positional encoding method for a neural network architecture called the Transformer. Unlike the standard sinusoidal positional encoding, our approach is based on solid mathematical grounds and has a guarantee of not losing information about the positional order of the input sequence. We show that the new encoding approach systematically improves the prediction performance in the time-series classification task.

papers.title: ERNIE-Tiny : A Progressive Distillation Framework for Pretrained Transformer Compression
papers.research_question: How to effectively compress pretrained language models (PLMs) by addressing the pretrain-finetune distillation discrepancy through a smooth transition of teacher, training data, and learning objective?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a four-stage progressive distillation framework (ERNIE-Tiny) that smooths the transition from pretrain to finetune distillation by gradually altering teacher model, training data, and learning objective, introducing a novel general-enhanced distillation stage to improve student generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny effectively compresses pretrained language models, maintaining high performance while significantly reducing model size and inference time, and demonstrates improved generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny student maintains over 98% of its 12-layer teacher BERTbase performance on the GLUE benchmark with 9.4x faster inference speed.
The general-enhanced distillation stage, which uses a finetuned teacher on general data, improves the student model's generalization, especially on low-resource tasks.
The task-adaptive distillation stage serves as a crucial bridge, smoothing the transition between general and task-specific data distillation and improving final performance.
ERNIE-Tiny achieves state-of-the-art compression results on both English (GLUE) and Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming the teacher BERTbase on Chinese tasks with 7.5x fewer parameters.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of each distillation stage, with the removal of any stage leading to performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The work did not apply larger unlabeled general data such as C4, leaving more efficient data utilization for future work.
future_direction: Applying larger unlabeled general data (e.g., C4) and exploring more efficient data utilization.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) such as BERT adopt a training paradigm which first pretrain the model in general data and then finetune the model on task-specific data, and have recently achieved great success. However, PLMs are notorious for their enormous parameters and hard to be deployed on real-life applications. Knowledge distillation has been prevailing to address this problem by transferring knowledge from a large teacher to a much smaller student over a set of data. We argue that the selection of thee three key components, namely teacher, training data, and learning objective, is crucial to the effectiveness of distillation. We, therefore, propose a four-stage progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny to compress PLM, which varies the three components gradually from general level to task-specific level. Specifically, the first stage, General Distillation, performs distillation with guidance from pretrained teacher, gerenal data and latent distillation loss. Then, General-Enhanced Distillation changes teacher model from pretrained teacher to finetuned teacher. After that, Task-Adaptive Distillation shifts training data from general data to task-specific data. In the end, Task-Specific Distillation, adds two additional losses, namely Soft-Label and Hard-Label loss onto the last stage. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework and generalization gain brought by ERNIE-Tiny.In particular, experiments show that a 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny maintains over 98.0%performance of its 12-layer teacher BERT base on GLUE benchmark, surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) by 1.0% GLUE score with the same amount of parameters. Moreover, ERNIE-Tiny achieves a new compression SOTA on five Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming BERT base by 0.4% accuracy with 7.5x fewer parameters and9.4x faster inference speed.

papers.title: How Does Selective Mechanism Improve Self-Attention Networks?
papers.research_question: How does the selective mechanism improve self-attention networks (SANs)? Specifically, what are the underlying reasons for the strong performance of selective SANs?
papers.core_contribution: The selective mechanism, implemented via Gumbel-Softmax, improves self-attention networks by mitigating their weaknesses in word order encoding and syntactic structure modeling, primarily by focusing attention on semantically important content words.
papers.conclusion: The selective mechanism mitigates two major weaknesses of self-attention networks—word order encoding and structure modeling—by enabling the model to focus on content words, which is essential for natural language understanding and generation.
papers.key_findings:
SSANs consistently outperform standard SANs on multiple NLP tasks (natural language inference, semantic role labeling, machine translation).
SSANs improve the ability to capture both local and global word order information, as shown by higher accuracy on word reordering detection tasks.
SSANs produce more syntactic representations and better model sentence structure, as evidenced by improved performance on linguistic probing tasks (TreeDepth, TopConst).
The selective mechanism helps SANs by paying more attention to content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) and less to function words (prepositions, determiners, punctuation).
Applying the selective mechanism to the first encoder layer yields the most significant improvements for word order tasks, suggesting lexical information is crucial.
papers.limitation: The findings are validated on specific SAN architectures and tasks; their generalizability to other architectures (e.g., BERT) and more general attention models remains to be explored.
future_direction: Validating the findings on other SAN architectures (e.g., BERT).
Extending the analysis to more general attention models.
papers.abstract: Self-attention networks (SANs) with selective mechanism has produced substantial improvements in various NLP tasks by concentrating on a subset of input words. However, the underlying reasons for their strong performance have not been well explained. In this paper, we bridge the gap by assessing the strengths of selective SANs (SSANs), which are implemented with a flexible and universal Gumbel-Softmax. Experimental results on several representative NLP tasks, including natural language inference, semantic role labelling, and machine translation, show that SSANs consistently outperform the standard SANs. Through well-designed probing experiments, we empirically validate that the improvement of SSANs can be attributed in part to mitigating two commonly-cited weaknesses of SANs: word order encoding and structure modeling. Specifically, the selective mechanism improves SANs by paying more attention to content words that contribute to the meaning of the sentence. The code and data are released at https://github.com/xwgeng/SSAN.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Improving Transformer Models by Reordering their Sublayers
papers.research_question: Whether reordering the self-attention and feedforward sublayers in a transformer can lead to better performance, and what patterns are beneficial.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reordering transformer sublayers can improve performance, and proposes the sandwich transformer pattern (more self-attention at the bottom, more feedforward at the top) which improves language modeling performance at no extra cost.
papers.conclusion: Sublayer reordering can improve transformer performance at no extra cost, but the optimal ordering may be task-dependent, suggesting further exploration for other tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly reordering transformer sublayers can yield models that outperform the standard interleaved baseline.
Better performing models tend to have more self-attention sublayers at the bottom and more feedforward sublayers at the top.
The proposed sandwich transformer pattern improves perplexity on word-level and character-level language modeling benchmarks.
The sandwich pattern does not improve performance on machine translation, indicating task-specific optimal orderings may exist.
Attention patterns differ between sandwich and baseline models, as measured by Earth Mover's Distance.
papers.limitation:
The sandwich reordering pattern does not guarantee performance gains across every task, as demonstrated on machine translation models.
No explanation is provided for why the sandwich pattern improves language modeling performance.
future_direction: Exploring task-specific sublayer reorderings for tasks like translation, question answering, and classification.
Applying neural architecture search methods to the sublayer ordering problem.
papers.abstract: Multilayer transformer networks consist of interleaved self-attention and feedforward sublayers. Could ordering the sublayers in a different pattern lead to better performance? We generate randomly ordered transformers and train them with the language modeling objective. We observe that some of these models are able to achieve better performance than the interleaved baseline, and that those successful variants tend to have more self-attention at the bottom and more feedforward sublayers at the top. We propose a new transformer pattern that adheres to this property, the sandwich transformer, and show that it improves perplexity on multiple word-level and character-level language modeling benchmarks, at no cost in parameters, memory, or training time. However, the sandwich reordering pattern does not guarantee performance gains across every task, as we demonstrate on machine translation models. Instead, we suggest that further exploration of task-specific sublayer reorderings is needed in order to unlock additional gains. 1

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: VISIT: Visualizing and Interpreting the Semantic Information Flow of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and visualize the semantic information flow inside transformer language models, particularly focusing on attention heads and memory values?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a tool for visualizing the semantic information flow in transformer language models as an interactive flow graph, and provides new insights into layer norms as semantic filters and the existence of regularization neurons.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces a tool to visualize the semantic information flow in transformers using the logit lens, demonstrates its utility by revealing insights about layer norms and regularization neurons, and validates the approach by supporting other analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads' semantics can be projected via the OV circuit, and only the heads with the largest norms dominate the block's output.
Memory values with the highest attention scores capture the semantics of their corresponding attention head.
Layer normalization layers act as semantic filters, demoting function words and promoting content words in the residual stream.
Regularization neurons exist that are consistently highly activated, have high entropy, and may serve as a constant bias or regularization term.
The flow-graph visualization tool can qualitatively replicate mechanistic analyses, such as indirect object identification, and reveal internal information flow patterns.
papers.limitation:
Limited to English language models, particularly GPT models with multi-head attention, and insights might not generalize to other languages or datasets.
Projection methods and the intersection score Ik have limitations in capturing semantic connections between different tokens with the same meaning.
Pruning based on the assumption that the most activated neurons determine the final prediction might be misleading as less activated neurons could also be relevant.
The methods are not causal and do not employ interventions, so further investigation is needed to fully understand the mechanisms.
future_direction: Apply causal interventions to verify the findings.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in interpretability suggest we can project weights and hidden states of transformer-based language models (LMs) to their vocabulary, a transformation that makes them more human interpretable. In this paper, we investigate LM attention heads and memory values, the vectors the models dynamically create and recall while processing a given input. By analyzing the tokens they represent through this projection, we identify patterns in the information flow inside the attention mechanism. Based on our discoveries, we create a tool to visualize a forward pass of Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs) as an interactive flow graph, with nodes representing neurons or hidden states and edges representing the interactions between them. Our visualization simplifies huge amounts of data into easy-to-read plots that can reflect the models' internal processing, uncovering the contribution of each component to the models' final prediction. Our visualization also unveils new insights about the role of layer norms as semantic filters that influence the models' output, and about neurons that are always activated during forward passes and act as regularization vectors.

papers.title: Breaking Symmetry When Training Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures obtain positional information without positional encodings, and what is the role of causal attention and residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Investigates the role of causal attention and residual connections in enabling Transformers to model positional information without positional encodings, finding that causal attention is necessary and residual connections aid convergence.
papers.conclusion: Causal attention is necessary for Transformers to model positional information without encodings; residual connections improve convergence but their role in preserving positional information is not definitively proven.
papers.key_findings:
Without causal attention, Transformer predictions are invariant to permutations of input tokens.
Causal attention is sufficient to break symmetry and enable modeling of input sequence order.
Residual connections are necessary for convergence when training Transformers without positional encodings.
Ablating too many residual connections prevents convergence on the three-digit addition task.
Correlation matrices suggest residual connections may help preserve positional information, but definitive evidence is lacking.
papers.limitation:
Experiments do not provide definitive evidence on whether residual connections help store positional information or merely help with convergence properties.
Negative convergence results might be due to insufficient hyperparameter tuning or training duration.
future_direction: Investigate the role of residual connections in preserving positional information while controlling for convergence effects.
papers.abstract: As we show in this paper, the prediction for output token $n+1$ of Transformer architectures without one of the mechanisms of positional encodings and causal attention is invariant to permutations of input tokens $1, 2, ..., n-1$. Usually, both mechanisms are employed and the symmetry with respect to the input tokens is broken. Recently, it has been shown that one can train Transformers without positional encodings. This must be enabled by the causal attention mechanism. In this paper, we elaborate on the argument that the causal connection mechanism must be responsible for the fact that Transformers are able to model input sequences where the order is important. Vertical "slices" of Transformers are all encouraged to represent the same location $k$ in the input sequence. We hypothesize that residual connections contribute to this phenomenon, and demonstrate evidence for this.

papers.title: Revisiting LRP: Positional Attribution as the Missing Ingredient for Transformer Explainability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional encoding into LRP-based explainability methods for Transformers to improve faithfulness and conservation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that existing LRP-based explainability methods for Transformers overlook positional encoding, leading to violation of conservation and loss of positional relevance. It proposes PA-LRP, a method that reformulates the input space and introduces PE-aware LRP rules, significantly improving explainability performance.
papers.conclusion: Positional-associated relevance carries a unique type of significance and is crucial for Transformer explainability; PA-LRP effectively incorporates it, improving XAI methods.
papers.key_findings:
PA-LRP outperforms the state-of-the-art AttnLRP method in perturbation tests across both NLP and vision tasks.
The positional-only relevance (PE Only) is significant and sometimes outperforms AttnLRP, demonstrating the importance of PE-associated signal.
The multi-sink mechanism for aggregating relevance across layers improves results.
Qualitative analysis shows that PE-associated relevance captures unique spatial, positional, and structural patterns, complementing semantic relevance.
Theoretical analysis proves that ignoring PE violates the conservation property and leads to unfaithful explanations.
papers.limitation: The work does not extend this insight to redesign or systematically revisit existing LRP rules for attention mechanisms and Transformer models, which could lead to further improvements.
papers.abstract: The development of effective explainability tools for Transformers is a crucial pursuit in deep learning research. One of the most promising approaches in this domain is Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), which propagates relevance scores backward through the network to the input space by redistributing activation values based on predefined rules. However, existing LRP-based methods for Transformer explainability entirely overlook a critical component of the Transformer architecture: its positional encoding (PE), resulting in violation of the conservation property, and the loss of an important and unique type of relevance, which is also associated with structural and positional features. To address this limitation, we reformulate the input space for Transformer explainability as a set of position-token pairs. This allows us to propose specialized theoretically-grounded LRP rules designed to propagate attributions across various positional encoding methods, including Rotary, Learnable, and Absolute PE. Extensive experiments with both fine-tuned classifiers and zero-shot foundation models, such as LLaMA 3, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in both vision and NLP explainability tasks. Our code is publicly available.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Dynamical Properties of Tokens in Self-Attention and Effects of Positional Encoding
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical properties of tokens in the continuous-time limit of pre-trained Transformer self-attention, and how do different positional encodings affect these dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of token dynamics in self-attention, deriving conditions under which tokens converge or diverge, and shows that convergence harms model performance. It then proposes simple architectural refinements to mitigate convergence in Transformers with absolute or rotary positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical and empirical analysis of token dynamics provides insights for improving Transformer architectures, and the proposed refinements to positional encoding schemes effectively mitigate harmful convergence behavior.
papers.key_findings:
When the matrix A (defined as W*(V^T)^{-1}) is negative definite and W is positive definite, tokens converge to zero, which negatively impacts model performance.
Absolute positional encoding has minimal effect on token dynamics, while rotary positional encoding encourages token divergence.
Empirical validation on language and vision tasks shows that constraining models to a divergence regime improves performance over baseline and convergence regimes.
In the divergence scenario, tokens organize into a small number of groups, with tokens within the same group diverging to infinity in a consistent direction.
Simple refinements to the query-key interaction matrix in rotary positional encoding can shift the dynamics from convergence to divergence, leading to improved performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis omits other token-wise operations such as layer normalization and feed-forward networks, and assumes time-invariant parameters for analytical simplicity.
The continuous-time limit may not fully capture the discrete-layer behavior of practical Transformers, especially when LayerNorm and FFNs are present.
future_direction: Extend the theoretical framework to incorporate layer normalization and feed-forward networks.
Apply the dynamical analysis to other architectures beyond standard Transformers.
Investigate the effects of other positional encoding schemes on token dynamics.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamical properties of tokens in pre-trained Transformer models and explores their application to improving Transformers. To this end, we analyze the dynamical system governing the continuous-time limit of the pre-trained model and characterize the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. Specifically, we characterize when tokens move closer to or farther from one another over time, depending on the model parameters. We provide sufficient conditions, based on these parameters, to identify scenarios where tokens either converge to zero or diverge to infinity. Unlike prior works, our conditions are broader in scope and more applicable to real-world models. Furthermore, we investigate how different forms of positional encoding -- specifically absolute and rotary -- affect these dynamical regimes. Empirical evidence reveals that the convergence scenario adversely impacts model performance. Motivated by these insights, we propose simple refinements to Transformer architectures that mitigate convergence behavior in models with absolute or rotary positional encoding. These findings support theoretical foundations and design principles for improving Transformer models.

papers.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Learning Syntax Without Planting Trees: Understanding Hierarchical Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do transformers show hierarchical generalization, despite lacking architectural biases towards hierarchical structure?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the language modeling objective consistently leads transformers to generalize hierarchically on synthetic tasks, and provides a Bayesian explanation linking this preference to the simplicity of hierarchical grammars.
papers.conclusion: The language modeling objective is a key inductive bias for hierarchical generalization in transformers, and a Bayesian perspective explains this preference via the simplicity of hierarchical grammars.
papers.key_findings:
The language modeling objective consistently leads to hierarchical generalization across five synthetic tasks, while other objectives like sequence-to-sequence modeling often fail.
Subnetworks implementing hierarchical and linear generalizations coexist within the trained transformer and persist throughout training.
The coexistence of subnetworks is due to ambiguous training data; adding disambiguating examples causes the linear subnetwork to disappear.
A Bayesian analysis shows that transformers generalize hierarchically when hierarchical grammars have higher posterior probability than regular grammars, indicating a preference for simpler explanations.
In a low-diversity dataset where regular grammars have higher posterior, transformers fail to generalize hierarchically, confirming the correlation.
papers.limitation:
The study only considers synthetic datasets and small transformer models; it is unclear if findings extend to larger models trained on natural language corpora.
The Bayesian analysis relies on hand-constructed grammars and specific prior choices; while sensitivity analysis is performed, other priors could lead to different conclusions.
The pruning method only considers attention heads; other components like MLPs are not included.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to larger transformer models trained on natural language corpora.
Include other model components beyond attention heads in pruning and analysis.
Apply the Bayesian framework to study other forms of generalization in language models.
papers.abstract: Transformers trained on natural language data have been shown to learn its hierarchical structure and generalize to sentences with unseen syntactic structures without explicitly encoding any structural bias. In this work, we investigate sources of inductive bias in transformer models and their training that could cause such generalization behavior to emerge. We extensively experiment with transformer models trained on multiple synthetic datasets and with different training objectives and show that while other objectives e.g. sequence-to-sequence modeling, prefix language modeling, often failed to lead to hierarchical generalization, models trained with the language modeling objective consistently learned to generalize hierarchically. We then conduct pruning experiments to study how transformers trained with the language modeling objective encode hierarchical structure. When pruned, we find joint existence of subnetworks within the model with different generalization behaviors (subnetworks corresponding to hierarchical structure and linear order). Finally, we take a Bayesian perspective to further uncover transformers' preference for hierarchical generalization: We establish a correlation between whether transformers generalize hierarchically on a dataset and whether the simplest explanation of that dataset is provided by a hierarchical grammar compared to regular grammars exhibiting linear generalization.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: On Scalar Embedding of Relative Positions in Attention Models
papers.research_question: Why does scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) work well in attention models, and how can it be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a probabilistic interpretation of T5's scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) as defining a prior distribution over relative positions, and proposes AT5, a new SRPE method with a learnable bucketing function and constrained bucket embeddings, which outperforms T5 on several tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a probabilistic interpretation of T5's SRPE, identifies its limitations, and proposes the AT5 model which improves upon T5 and may apply to other NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SRPE in attention can be interpreted as defining a prior distribution over relative positions, with the final attentive distribution being the posterior given the input sequence.
T5's SRPE has two weaknesses: a fixed heuristic bucketing function and independent bucket embeddings, which can lead to underfitting and overfitting respectively.
The proposed AT5 model, with a learnable bucketing function and MLP-constrained embeddings, achieves superior performance to T5 on artificial tasks, text classification, question answering, and machine translation.
Quantitative analysis shows AT5 learns more meaningful prior probability distributions over relative positions compared to T5.
Ablation studies indicate that higher-probability heads in AT5 contribute more to its performance gain compared to T5.
papers.abstract: Attention with positional encoding has been demonstrated as a powerful component in modern neural network models, such as transformers. However, why positional encoding works well in attention models remains largely unanswered. In this paper, we study the scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) proposed in the T5 transformer. Such an encoding method has two features. First, it uses a scalar to embed relative positions. Second, the relative positions are bucketized using a fixed heuristic algorithm, and positions in the same bucket share the same embedding. In this work, we show that SRPE in attention has an elegant probabilistic interpretation. More specifically, the positional encoding serves to produce a prior distribution for the attended positions. The resulting attentive distribution can be viewed as a posterior distribution of the attended position given the observed input sequence. Furthermore, we propose a new SRPE (AT5) that adopts a learnable bucketization protocol and automatically adapts to the dependency range specific to the learning task. Empirical studies show that the AT5 achieves superior performance than the T5's SRPE.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Exploring Context Window of Large Language Models via Decomposed Positional Vectors
papers.research_question: How is positional information formed and represented in LLMs, and how can we extend the context window by manipulating positional vectors?
papers.core_contribution: We analyze the formation and effect of positional vectors in LLMs and propose two training-free methods to extend the context window by interpolating positional vectors.
papers.conclusion: We explored the mechanism of LLMs' context window via decomposed positional vectors and proposed two training-free extension methods, which we believe will promote better algorithms for context window extension.
papers.key_findings:
Initial tokens form distinct positional vectors and serve as anchors for shaping positional vectors of subsequent tokens.
Positional vectors play a critical role in modulating long-term decay and establishing attention sinks.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) positional vectors beyond the context window cause performance degradation.
Length extrapolation methods maintain consistency of positional vectors within and beyond the context window.
Context window extension methods achieve interpolation of positional vectors by adjusting information flow from initial tokens.
papers.limitation: The study is constrained by the use of small-scale LLMs trained by the authors and the lack of suitable external models for validation.
future_direction: Validate findings on a broader range of models.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) typically have a limited context window, resulting in significant performance degradation when processing text beyond the length of the context window. Extensive studies have been proposed to extend the context window and achieve length extrapolation of LLMs, but there is still a lack of in-depth interpretation of these approaches. In this study, we explore the positional information within and beyond the context window for deciphering the underlying mechanism of LLMs. By using a mean-based decomposition method, we disentangle positional vectors from hidden states of LLMs and analyze their formation and effect on attention. Furthermore, when texts exceed the context window, we analyze the change of positional vectors in two settings, i.e., direct extrapolation and context window extension. Based on our findings, we design two training-free context window extension methods, positional vector replacement and attention window extension. Experimental results show that our methods can effectively extend the context window length.

papers.title: Unveiling the Magic: Investigating Attention Distillation in Retrieval-augmented Generation
papers.research_question: What are the key factors and patterns that make attention distillation effective in training retrieval-augmented language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes attention distillation in retrieval-augmented generation, identifying that attention to answer and question-related tokens is crucial, and proposes metrics to assess distillation quality for better training.
