This must be enabled by the causal attention mechanism. In this paper, we elaborate on the argument that the causal connection mechanism must be responsible for the fact that Transformers are able to model input sequences where the order is important. Vertical "slices" of Transformers are all encouraged to represent the same location $k$ in the input sequence. We hypothesize that residual connections contribute to this phenomenon, and demonstrate evidence for this.

papers.title: Revisiting LRP: Positional Attribution as the Missing Ingredient for Transformer Explainability
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional encoding into LRP-based explainability methods for Transformers to improve faithfulness and conservation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that existing LRP-based explainability methods for Transformers overlook positional encoding, leading to violation of conservation and loss of positional relevance. It proposes PA-LRP, a method that reformulates the input space and introduces PE-aware LRP rules, significantly improving explainability performance.
papers.conclusion: Positional-associated relevance carries a unique type of significance and is crucial for Transformer explainability; PA-LRP effectively incorporates it, improving XAI methods.
papers.key_findings:
PA-LRP outperforms the state-of-the-art AttnLRP method in perturbation tests across both NLP and vision tasks.
The positional-only relevance (PE Only) is significant and sometimes outperforms AttnLRP, demonstrating the importance of PE-associated signal.
The multi-sink mechanism for aggregating relevance across layers improves results.
Qualitative analysis shows that PE-associated relevance captures unique spatial, positional, and structural patterns, complementing semantic relevance.
Theoretical analysis proves that ignoring PE violates the conservation property and leads to unfaithful explanations.
papers.limitation: The work does not extend this insight to redesign or systematically revisit existing LRP rules for attention mechanisms and Transformer models, which could lead to further improvements.
papers.abstract: The development of effective explainability tools for Transformers is a crucial pursuit in deep learning research. One of the most promising approaches in this domain is Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), which propagates relevance scores backward through the network to the input space by redistributing activation values based on predefined rules. However, existing LRP-based methods for Transformer explainability entirely overlook a critical component of the Transformer architecture: its positional encoding (PE), resulting in violation of the conservation property, and the loss of an important and unique type of relevance, which is also associated with structural and positional features. To address this limitation, we reformulate the input space for Transformer explainability as a set of position-token pairs. This allows us to propose specialized theoretically-grounded LRP rules designed to propagate attributions across various positional encoding methods, including Rotary, Learnable, and Absolute PE. Extensive experiments with both fine-tuned classifiers and zero-shot foundation models, such as LLaMA 3, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in both vision and NLP explainability tasks. Our code is publicly available.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Dynamical Properties of Tokens in Self-Attention and Effects of Positional Encoding
papers.research_question: What are the dynamical properties of tokens in the continuous-time limit of pre-trained Transformer self-attention, and how do different positional encodings affect these dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of token dynamics in self-attention, deriving conditions under which tokens converge or diverge, and shows that convergence harms model performance. It then proposes simple architectural refinements to mitigate convergence in Transformers with absolute or rotary positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical and empirical analysis of token dynamics provides insights for improving Transformer architectures, and the proposed refinements to positional encoding schemes effectively mitigate harmful convergence behavior.
papers.key_findings:
When the matrix A (defined as W*(V^T)^{-1}) is negative definite and W is positive definite, tokens converge to zero, which negatively impacts model performance.
Absolute positional encoding has minimal effect on token dynamics, while rotary positional encoding encourages token divergence.
Empirical validation on language and vision tasks shows that constraining models to a divergence regime improves performance over baseline and convergence regimes.
In the divergence scenario, tokens organize into a small number of groups, with tokens within the same group diverging to infinity in a consistent direction.
Simple refinements to the query-key interaction matrix in rotary positional encoding can shift the dynamics from convergence to divergence, leading to improved performance.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical analysis omits other token-wise operations such as layer normalization and feed-forward networks, and assumes time-invariant parameters for analytical simplicity.
The continuous-time limit may not fully capture the discrete-layer behavior of practical Transformers, especially when LayerNorm and FFNs are present.
future_direction: Extend the theoretical framework to incorporate layer normalization and feed-forward networks.
Apply the dynamical analysis to other architectures beyond standard Transformers.
Investigate the effects of other positional encoding schemes on token dynamics.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the dynamical properties of tokens in pre-trained Transformer models and explores their application to improving Transformers. To this end, we analyze the dynamical system governing the continuous-time limit of the pre-trained model and characterize the asymptotic behavior of its solutions. Specifically, we characterize when tokens move closer to or farther from one another over time, depending on the model parameters. We provide sufficient conditions, based on these parameters, to identify scenarios where tokens either converge to zero or diverge to infinity. Unlike prior works, our conditions are broader in scope and more applicable to real-world models. Furthermore, we investigate how different forms of positional encoding -- specifically absolute and rotary -- affect these dynamical regimes. Empirical evidence reveals that the convergence scenario adversely impacts model performance. Motivated by these insights, we propose simple refinements to Transformer architectures that mitigate convergence behavior in models with absolute or rotary positional encoding. These findings support theoretical foundations and design principles for improving Transformer models.

papers.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Learning Syntax Without Planting Trees: Understanding Hierarchical Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: Why do transformers show hierarchical generalization, despite lacking architectural biases towards hierarchical structure?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the language modeling objective consistently leads transformers to generalize hierarchically on synthetic tasks, and provides a Bayesian explanation linking this preference to the simplicity of hierarchical grammars.
papers.conclusion: The language modeling objective is a key inductive bias for hierarchical generalization in transformers, and a Bayesian perspective explains this preference via the simplicity of hierarchical grammars.
papers.key_findings:
The language modeling objective consistently leads to hierarchical generalization across five synthetic tasks, while other objectives like sequence-to-sequence modeling often fail.
Subnetworks implementing hierarchical and linear generalizations coexist within the trained transformer and persist throughout training.
The coexistence of subnetworks is due to ambiguous training data; adding disambiguating examples causes the linear subnetwork to disappear.
A Bayesian analysis shows that transformers generalize hierarchically when hierarchical grammars have higher posterior probability than regular grammars, indicating a preference for simpler explanations.
In a low-diversity dataset where regular grammars have higher posterior, transformers fail to generalize hierarchically, confirming the correlation.
papers.limitation:
The study only considers synthetic datasets and small transformer models; it is unclear if findings extend to larger models trained on natural language corpora.
The Bayesian analysis relies on hand-constructed grammars and specific prior choices; while sensitivity analysis is performed, other priors could lead to different conclusions.
The pruning method only considers attention heads; other components like MLPs are not included.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to larger transformer models trained on natural language corpora.
Include other model components beyond attention heads in pruning and analysis.
Apply the Bayesian framework to study other forms of generalization in language models.
papers.abstract: Transformers trained on natural language data have been shown to learn its hierarchical structure and generalize to sentences with unseen syntactic structures without explicitly encoding any structural bias. In this work, we investigate sources of inductive bias in transformer models and their training that could cause such generalization behavior to emerge. We extensively experiment with transformer models trained on multiple synthetic datasets and with different training objectives and show that while other objectives e.g. sequence-to-sequence modeling, prefix language modeling, often failed to lead to hierarchical generalization, models trained with the language modeling objective consistently learned to generalize hierarchically. We then conduct pruning experiments to study how transformers trained with the language modeling objective encode hierarchical structure. When pruned, we find joint existence of subnetworks within the model with different generalization behaviors (subnetworks corresponding to hierarchical structure and linear order). Finally, we take a Bayesian perspective to further uncover transformers' preference for hierarchical generalization: We establish a correlation between whether transformers generalize hierarchically on a dataset and whether the simplest explanation of that dataset is provided by a hierarchical grammar compared to regular grammars exhibiting linear generalization.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: On Scalar Embedding of Relative Positions in Attention Models
papers.research_question: Why does scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) work well in attention models, and how can it be improved?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a probabilistic interpretation of T5's scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) as defining a prior distribution over relative positions, and proposes AT5, a new SRPE method with a learnable bucketing function and constrained bucket embeddings, which outperforms T5 on several tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a probabilistic interpretation of T5's SRPE, identifies its limitations, and proposes the AT5 model which improves upon T5 and may apply to other NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SRPE in attention can be interpreted as defining a prior distribution over relative positions, with the final attentive distribution being the posterior given the input sequence.
T5's SRPE has two weaknesses: a fixed heuristic bucketing function and independent bucket embeddings, which can lead to underfitting and overfitting respectively.
The proposed AT5 model, with a learnable bucketing function and MLP-constrained embeddings, achieves superior performance to T5 on artificial tasks, text classification, question answering, and machine translation.
Quantitative analysis shows AT5 learns more meaningful prior probability distributions over relative positions compared to T5.
Ablation studies indicate that higher-probability heads in AT5 contribute more to its performance gain compared to T5.
papers.abstract: Attention with positional encoding has been demonstrated as a powerful component in modern neural network models, such as transformers. However, why positional encoding works well in attention models remains largely unanswered. In this paper, we study the scalar relative positional encoding (SRPE) proposed in the T5 transformer. Such an encoding method has two features. First, it uses a scalar to embed relative positions. Second, the relative positions are bucketized using a fixed heuristic algorithm, and positions in the same bucket share the same embedding. In this work, we show that SRPE in attention has an elegant probabilistic interpretation. More specifically, the positional encoding serves to produce a prior distribution for the attended positions. The resulting attentive distribution can be viewed as a posterior distribution of the attended position given the observed input sequence. Furthermore, we propose a new SRPE (AT5) that adopts a learnable bucketization protocol and automatically adapts to the dependency range specific to the learning task. Empirical studies show that the AT5 achieves superior performance than the T5's SRPE.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Incorporating Residual and Normalization Layers into Analysis of Masked Language Models
papers.research_question: How do residual connections and layer normalization affect the context-mixing in Transformer attention blocks compared to attention alone?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends norm-based analysis to include residual and layer normalization layers in Transformer attention blocks, showing that the context-mixing ratio is much lower than previously estimated, indicating that residual connections and layer normalization dominate the information flow.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual connections and layer normalization significantly reduce the context-mixing effect of attention, leading to a much lower mixing ratio than previously assumed, which explains why discarding learned attention patterns often does not harm performance.
papers.key_findings:
The context-mixing ratio in attention blocks is much lower (16-19% on average) when considering residual and normalization layers compared to attention-only analysis (84-97%).
The preserving effect via residual connection is dominant over the mixing effect of attention.
The multi-head attention shrinks input vectors, and layer normalization further reduces the mixing ratio.
For masked tokens, the mixing ratio is higher in middle and later layers.
Larger BERT models show a negative correlation between word frequency and mixing ratio, indicating discounting of high-frequency words.
papers.limitation: Experiments limited to Transformer-based masked language models; feed-forward and embedding layers not analyzed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to other Transformer variants
Extend analysis to feed-forward and embedding layers
papers.abstract: Transformer architecture has become ubiquitous in the natural language processing field. To interpret the Transformer-based models, their attention patterns have been extensively analyzed. However, the Transformer architecture is not only composed of the multihead attention; other components can also contribute to Transformers' progressive performance. In this study, we extended the scope of the analysis of Transformers from solely the attention patterns to the whole attention block, i.e., multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization. Our analysis of Transformer-based masked language models shows that the token-to-token interaction performed via attention has less impact on the intermediate representations than previously assumed. These results provide new intuitive explanations of existing reports; for example, discarding the learned attention patterns tends not to adversely affect the performance. The codes of our experiments are publicly available.

papers.title: Label Words are Anchors: An Information Flow Perspective for Understanding In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning (ICL) work in large language models, specifically what is the role of label words in the information flow?
papers.core_contribution: Label words serve as anchors in in-context learning: they aggregate information from demonstrations in shallow layers and provide reference for predictions in deep layers.
papers.conclusion: Label words function as anchors in ICL, aggregating and distributing task-relevant information; this understanding enables improvements in accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Label words aggregate information from demonstration examples in shallow transformer layers.
The model extracts information from label words in deep layers to form the final prediction.
Anchor re-weighting, which adjusts the significance of label words, improves ICL accuracy by an average of 16.7%.
Compressing demonstrations to anchor hidden states (Hiddenanchor) speeds up inference by up to 1.8× with minimal performance loss.
ICL errors can be diagnosed by analyzing distances between anchor key vectors, which correlate with category confusion.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to classification tasks and does not explore generative tasks.
Due to hardware constraints, models are limited to up to 6 billion parameters, leaving larger-scale models unexplored.
The hypothesis is only examined in conventional ICL paradigms, not in others like chain-of-thought prompting.
future_direction: Replicating the study with larger-scale models.
Exploring other ICL paradigms such as chain-of-thought prompting.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) emerges as a promising capability of large language models (LLMs) by providing them with demonstration examples to perform diverse tasks. However, the underlying mechanism of how LLMs learn from the provided context remains under-explored. In this paper, we investigate the working mechanism of ICL through an information flow lens. Our findings reveal that label words in the demonstration examples function as anchors: (1) semantic information aggregates into label word representations during the shallow computation layers' processing; (2) the consolidated information in label words serves as a reference for LLMs' final predictions. Based on these insights, we introduce an anchor re-weighting method to improve ICL performance, a demonstration compression technique to expedite inference, and an analysis framework for diagnosing ICL errors in GPT2-XL. The promising applications of our findings again validate the uncovered ICL working mechanism and pave the way for future studies.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Exploring Context Window of Large Language Models via Decomposed Positional Vectors
papers.research_question: How is positional information formed and represented in LLMs, and how can we extend the context window by manipulating positional vectors?
papers.core_contribution: We analyze the formation and effect of positional vectors in LLMs and propose two training-free methods to extend the context window by interpolating positional vectors.
papers.conclusion: We explored the mechanism of LLMs' context window via decomposed positional vectors and proposed two training-free extension methods, which we believe will promote better algorithms for context window extension.
papers.key_findings:
Initial tokens form distinct positional vectors and serve as anchors for shaping positional vectors of subsequent tokens.
Positional vectors play a critical role in modulating long-term decay and establishing attention sinks.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) positional vectors beyond the context window cause performance degradation.
Length extrapolation methods maintain consistency of positional vectors within and beyond the context window.
Context window extension methods achieve interpolation of positional vectors by adjusting information flow from initial tokens.
papers.limitation: The study is constrained by the use of small-scale LLMs trained by the authors and the lack of suitable external models for validation.
future_direction: Validate findings on a broader range of models.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) typically have a limited context window, resulting in significant performance degradation when processing text beyond the length of the context window. Extensive studies have been proposed to extend the context window and achieve length extrapolation of LLMs, but there is still a lack of in-depth interpretation of these approaches. In this study, we explore the positional information within and beyond the context window for deciphering the underlying mechanism of LLMs. By using a mean-based decomposition method, we disentangle positional vectors from hidden states of LLMs and analyze their formation and effect on attention. Furthermore, when texts exceed the context window, we analyze the change of positional vectors in two settings, i.e., direct extrapolation and context window extension. Based on our findings, we design two training-free context window extension methods, positional vector replacement and attention window extension. Experimental results show that our methods can effectively extend the context window length.

papers.title: Unveiling the Magic: Investigating Attention Distillation in Retrieval-augmented Generation
papers.research_question: What are the key factors and patterns that make attention distillation effective in training retrieval-augmented language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes attention distillation in retrieval-augmented generation, identifying that attention to answer and question-related tokens is crucial, and proposes metrics to assess distillation quality for better training.
papers.conclusion: The paper comprehensively evaluates attention distillation, emphasizing the importance of attention to answer and question-related tokens, and introduces novel metrics to assess attention distillation ability for optimizing training.
papers.key_findings:
Attention distillation effectiveness depends on reader quality; low-quality readers yield poor supervision.
High-quality readers show higher attention to answer-related tokens and question nouns.
Proposed indicators can evaluate attention distillation quality in decoder-only models.
Indicators may not fully apply to encoder-decoder models or perplexity distillation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is based on lightweight language models (about one billion parameters) and has not been extended to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Validating the methods on larger-scale language models.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation framework can address the limitations of large language models by enabling real-time knowledge updates for more accurate answers. An efficient way in the training phase of retrieval-augmented models is attention distillation, which uses attention scores as a supervision signal instead of manually annotated query-document pairs. Despite its growing popularity, the detailed mechanisms behind the success of attention distillation remain unexplored, particularly the specific patterns it leverages to benefit training. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive review of attention distillation workflow and identifying key factors influencing the learning quality of retrieval-augmented language models. We further propose indicators for optimizing models' training methods and avoiding ineffective training.

papers.title: Insights into LLM Long-Context Failures: When Transformers Know but Don't Tell
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to utilize information from the middle or end of long contexts, despite encoding that information internally?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies a 'know but don't tell' phenomenon in LLMs, where models encode the position of target information in their hidden representations but often fail to leverage this knowledge to generate accurate responses, especially for information in the middle of long contexts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs capture context information internally but fail to generate correct answers due to positional bias, and delayed extraction of information (requiring more layers) leads to lower generation accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
There is a gap between probing accuracy (internal knowledge) and generation accuracy (output): LLMs can locate information internally but fail to generate correct answers.
Middle-context information requires more transformer layers to be located compared to information at the beginning or end.
The earlier a model locates target information within its layers (shallower peak probing layer), the higher its final generation accuracy for that information.
Positional bias emerges during the model's internal processing, with a noticeable shift in logits at a certain layer depending on the position of the gold information.
papers.limitation: Knowledge of the gold document's location and the ability to cite from it are distinct; the model might know the location but still fail to integrate it into a coherent and accurate answer. The probing comparison does not fully capture the nuanced interactions between the model's internal attention mechanisms and output generation capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit positional bias, struggling to utilize information from the middle or end of long contexts. Our study explores LLMs' long-context reasoning by probing their hidden representations. We find that while LLMs encode the position of target information, they often fail to leverage this in generating accurate responses. This reveals a disconnect between information retrieval and utilization, a "know but don't tell" phenomenon. We further analyze the relationship between extraction time and final accuracy, offering insights into the underlying mechanics of transformer models.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: Round and Round We Go! What makes Rotary Positional Encodings useful?
papers.research_question: What makes Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE) useful, and how are they used mechanistically in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that Gemma uses RoPE's high frequencies for robust positional attention patterns and low frequencies for semantic information, and proposes p-RoPE, a modification that truncates low frequencies to improve performance.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a nuanced understanding of RoPE in LLMs, which is crucial for scaling to large context lengths, and the proposed p-RoPE modification shows promise for performance gains.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE does not necessarily decay attention with distance; this decay only occurs under specific conditions (e.g., constant queries and keys).
Gemma 7B prefers to use the low frequencies of RoPE for semantic information, while high frequencies are used for positional attention patterns.
High frequencies enable the construction of robust positional attention heads (e.g., diagonal and previous-token heads).
Low frequencies act as semantic channels but are not robust over long contexts due to rotation.
Truncating the lowest frequencies (p-RoPE) can improve performance and robustness in language modeling.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretations may not cover the entire spectrum of how LLMs use RoPE.
The evaluation of p-RoPE is limited to 2B parameter models and perplexity, which may not reflect downstream performance.
future_direction: More careful evaluation of p-RoPE on larger models and downstream tasks.
Analyzing other positional encodings (e.g., Alibi) in a similar mechanistic way.
Testing the effect of randomized positional encodings on frequency usage.
papers.abstract: Positional Encodings (PEs) are a critical component of Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs), providing the attention mechanism with important sequence-position information. One of the most popular types of encoding used today in LLMs are Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE), that rotate the queries and keys based on their relative distance. A common belief is that RoPE is useful because it helps to decay token dependency as relative distance increases. In this work, we argue that this is unlikely to be the core reason. We study the internals of a trained Gemma 7B model to understand how RoPE is being used at a mechanical level. We find that Gemma learns to use RoPE to construct robust "positional" attention patterns by exploiting the highest frequencies. We also find that, in general, Gemma greatly prefers to use the lowest frequencies of RoPE, which we suspect are used to carry semantic information. We mathematically prove interesting behaviours of RoPE and conduct experiments to verify our findings, proposing a modification of RoPE that fixes some highlighted issues and improves performance. We believe that this work represents an interesting step in better understanding PEs in LLMs, which we believe holds crucial value for scaling LLMs to large sizes and context lengths.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations
papers.research_question: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? How do transformers resolve the conflict between optimal Bayesian belief updating (a recursive process) and their parallelized, attention-driven architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. It explains why specific intermediate geometric structures emerge in transformer representations.
papers.conclusion: The geometric structures in transformer representations are a mathematical signature of how architectural constraints warp optimal Bayesian inference, revealing a precise interplay between theoretical necessity and implementation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating due to architectural constraints, bending optimal Bayesian inference into attention's parallelizable form.
The attention mechanism in the first layer implements a spectral algorithm that builds constrained beliefs, with attention weights approximating the decay of influence via eigenvalues of the data-generating transition matrix.
Intermediate representations (after attention) are fractals matching the constrained belief geometry, while final representations (after MLP) match the full, unconstrained belief geometry.
The attention pattern, OV vectors, and token embeddings can be theoretically predicted from the constrained belief updating equations.
For negative eigenvalues in the transition matrix (oscillatory dynamics), multiple attention heads are required to capture the full update pattern due to the non-negativity constraint of attention.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted on a tractable family of hidden Markov models (Mess3), which is a simplified setting.
As the HMM parameter α moves away from a central range, deviations between predicted and actual representations increase, and a complete characterization of these deviations remains for future work.
future_direction: A complete characterization of how deviations between predicted and actual representations scale with the HMM parameter α.
Applying the methodology to more complex cases, such as large language models trained on natural text, where the same tension between architecture and optimal inference is anticipated.
papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Rotary Offset Features in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are rotary offset features in large language models and how do they influence attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of rotary offset features in LLMs with rotary positional embeddings and derives bounds that predict their occurrence and properties.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals consistent patterns of rotary offset features across model architectures and scales, and the derived bounds can help improve understanding, context length extension, and quantization for models using rotary embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Rotary offset features (large-magnitude features in rotary feature pairs) exist consistently across layers, heads, and model architectures.
These features are found at low rotary frequencies that do not complete a full period within the context length.
An upper bound on the rotary frequency predicts which frequencies give rise to rotary offset features.
A lower bound predicts the minimum angle between query-key pairs for rotary offset features.
Rotary offset features influence attention patterns, including the selection of attention sinks.
future_direction: Altering the distribution of rotary frequencies to make LLMs adopt context length extension more effectively.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on positional encodings to provide sequence position information to their attention mechanism. Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE), which encode relative position by rotating queries and keys, have become widely used in modern LLMs. We study the features and patterns that emerge in queries and keys when using rotary embeddings and introduce the concept of rotary offset features. Our analysis reveals that these features, which frequently exhibit large activations and are often interpreted as outliers, arise consistently across layers, attention heads, and model architectures. We derive bounds predicting which rotary frequencies give rise to rotary offset features and the minimum angle between the query-key pairs for these features. We verify our predictions empirically across models of different sizes and architectures.

papers.title: The Generalization Ridge: Information Flow in Natural Language Generation
papers.research_question: In NLG, how does information evolve across layers during training, and how are different layers of the network functionally organized to support generalization versus memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, and uses it to reveal a 'generalization ridge' in intermediate layers where predictive information peaks, indicating a trade-off between generalization and memorization.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal a consistent generalization ridge in intermediate layers, reflecting a fundamental trade-off between generalization and memorization as information flows deeper into the model.
papers.key_findings:
Predictive information peaks at intermediate layers (the 'generalization ridge') and then declines in final layers.
Incremental information gain is highest in intermediate layers.
Attention patterns show that intermediate layers attend to task-relevant (signal) tokens.
Residual scaling experiments show that under distribution shift, the model relies less on final layers and more on intermediate layers.
The generalization ridge phenomenon persists in multi-token generation scenarios.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in natural language generation (NLG), yet their internal mechanisms for synthesizing task-relevant information remain insufficiently understood. While prior studies suggest that intermediate layers often yield more generalizable representations than final layers, how this generalization ability emerges and propagates across layers during training remains unclear. To address this gap, we propose InfoRidge, an information-theoretic framework, to characterize how predictive information-the mutual information between hidden representations and target outputs-varies across depth during training. Our experiments across various models and datasets reveal a consistent non-monotonic trend: predictive information peaks in intermediate layers-forming a generalization ridge-before declining in final layers, reflecting a transition between generalization and memorization. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conduct a set of complementary analyses that leverage residual scaling, attention pattern, and controlled model capacity to characterize layer-wise functional specialization. We further validate our findings with multiple-token generation experiments, verifying that the observed ridge phenomenon persists across decoding steps. Together, these findings offer new insights into the internal mechanisms of transformers and underscore the critical role of intermediate layers in supporting generalization.

papers.title: minicons: Enabling Flexible Behavioral and Representational Analyses of Transformer Language Models
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces minicons, an open-source library that provides a standard API for behavioral and representational analyses of transformer language models, facilitating efficient extraction of word/sentence probabilities and contextualized embeddings.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents minicons, a utility tool for analyzing transformer language models, and demonstrates its use in two case studies, showing its potential for facilitating behavioral and representational analyses.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's knowledge of linguistic acceptability emerges at different rates for different phenomena, with some phenomena showing signs of forgetting during training.
On zero-shot abductive reasoning, most models perform near chance, with ALBERT-xxlarge-v2 achieving the best accuracy (0.61) despite being smaller than other models.
Performance on abductive reasoning scales linearly with the logarithm of the number of parameters (R²=0.48), suggesting that scaling alone is unlikely to reach state-of-the-art performance.
future_direction: Integrate newer utility functions into the library and develop detailed tutorials for users.
papers.abstract: We present minicons, an open source library that provides a standard API for researchers interested in conducting behavioral and representational analyses of transformer-based language models (LMs). Specifically, minicons enables researchers to apply analysis methods at two levels: (1) at the prediction level -- by providing functions to efficiently extract word/sentence level probabilities; and (2) at the representational level -- by also facilitating efficient extraction of word/phrase level vectors from one or more layers. In this paper, we describe the library and apply it to two motivating case studies: One focusing on the learning dynamics of the BERT architecture on relative grammatical judgments, and the other on benchmarking 23 different LMs on zero-shot abductive reasoning. minicons is available at https://github.com/kanishkamisra/minicons

papers.title: Where meaning lives: Layer-wise accessibility of psycholinguistic features in encoder and decoder language models
papers.research_question: How are psychologically meaningful dimensions of language encoded across layers in transformer models, and how does this depend on embedding extraction methods and model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The apparent localization of psycholinguistic meaning in transformer models is strongly dependent on the embedding extraction method, and final-layer representations are rarely optimal for recovering this information with linear probes, despite a shared depth ordering of meaning dimensions across models.
papers.conclusion: Where meaning 'lives' in transformer models reflects an interaction between methodological choices (embedding extraction) and architectural constraints, with a robust lexico-semantic depth ordering shared across contemporary models.
papers.key_findings:
Contextualized embedding extraction methods (template, averaged) yield higher feature selectivity and different layer-wise profiles than isolated embeddings.
Final-layer representations are never optimal for recovering psycholinguistic information across all models and features; optimal layers are distributed throughout the network.
Models exhibit a shared depth ordering of meaning dimensions, with lexical properties peaking earlier and experiential/affective dimensions peaking later.
The degree to which psycholinguistic information is concentrated around optimal layers varies more by model than by architectural class (encoder vs. decoder).
Conclusions about where meaning is represented are contingent on the extraction strategy, with differences comparable in magnitude to differences between models or architectures.
papers.abstract: Understanding where transformer language models encode psychologically meaningful aspects of meaning is essential for both theory and practice. We conduct a systematic layer-wise probing study of 58 psycholinguistic features across 10 transformer models, spanning encoder-only and decoder-only architectures, and compare three embedding extraction methods. We find that apparent localization of meaning is strongly method-dependent: contextualized embeddings yield higher feature-specific selectivity and different layer-wise profiles than isolated embeddings. Across models and methods, final-layer representations are rarely optimal for recovering psycholinguistic information with linear probes. Despite these differences, models exhibit a shared depth ordering of meaning dimensions, with lexical properties peaking earlier and experiential and affective dimensions peaking later. Together, these results show that where meaning "lives" in transformer models reflects an interaction between methodological choices and architectural constraints.

papers.title: Systematic Generalization and Emergent Structures in Transformers Trained on Structured Tasks
papers.research_question: How and when can transformers acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer causal transformers with label-based order encoding can learn algorithmic tasks and generalize to longer sequences, exhibiting signs of task decomposition and shared computation across tasks.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve structured algorithmic tasks and generalize systematically, with attention layers developing task decomposition and shared computation.
papers.key_findings:
Label-based order encoding enables strong length generalization in transformers on algorithmic tasks.
Two-layer transformers are sufficient to solve multi-level sorting tasks, while single-layer models fail.
Attention patterns in two-layer models show task decomposition: first layer attends to items in the same feature group, second layer attends to the next output token.
In multi-task learning, transformers can learn multiple tasks simultaneously and generalize to longer sequences, with attention heads showing shared computation across tasks.
Task-conditioned item representations are reorganized according to the task structure, showing clustering by relevant features.
papers.limitation:
Label-based encoding alone would not represent true item distance information.
The tasks are simple and synthetic, and may not capture the complexity of natural data.
future_direction: Explore learning and generalization dynamics in transformer-based agents to understand the acquisition of task-conditioned, multi-level behavioral policies in structured environments.
Characterize the degree of possible computational modularity in multi-headed attention in relation to task structures.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks have seen great success in natural language processing and machine vision, where task objectives such as next word prediction and image classification benefit from nuanced context sensitivity across high-dimensional inputs. However, there is an ongoing debate about how and when transformers can acquire highly structured behavior and achieve systematic generalization. Here, we explore how well a causal transformer can perform a set of algorithmic tasks, including copying, sorting, and hierarchical compositions of these operations. We demonstrate strong generalization to sequences longer than those used in training by replacing the standard positional encoding typically used in transformers with labels arbitrarily paired with items in the sequence. We search for the layer and head configuration sufficient to solve these tasks, then probe for signs of systematic processing in latent representations and attention patterns. We show that two-layer transformers learn reliable solutions to multi-level problems, develop signs of task decomposition, and encode input items in a way that encourages the exploitation of shared computation across related tasks. These results provide key insights into how attention layers support structured computation both within a task and across multiple tasks.

papers.title: Can Transformers Learn Sequential Function Classes In Context?
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn from sequential, non-textual function class data distributions using in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can in-context learn sequential non-textual function classes, but this ability is less robust to label noise compared to textual tasks, indicating different underlying mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that transformers can learn sequential non-textual function classes in-context, providing a foundation for future studies on sequential data processing in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers are capable of in-context learning when trained on non-textual sequential function classes.
ICL performance degrades when y-labels are randomly permuted in non-textual sequential tasks.
Models retain some ICL capability even with randomized labels, showing robustness to noise.
The degradation suggests that ICL mechanisms may differ between textual and non-textual sequential data.
Transformers can learn and understand sequentiality in non-textual function class data distributions.
papers.limitation:
Limited compute power, training on small transformers with toy function classes.
Sequential functions were defined to be linearly separable, which may not generalize to more complex functions like language.
future_direction: Visualization of Induction Heads in relation to sequential function classes.
In-Context Learning with unstructured data to compare with structured data.
Exploration of Task Vectors and their role in in-context learning.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) has revolutionized the capabilities of transformer models in NLP. In our project, we extend the understanding of the mechanisms underpinning ICL by exploring whether transformers can learn from sequential, non-textual function class data distributions. We introduce a novel sliding window sequential function class and employ toy-sized transformers with a GPT-2 architecture to conduct our experiments. Our analysis indicates that these models can indeed leverage ICL when trained on non-textual sequential function classes. Additionally, our experiments with randomized y-label sequences highlights that transformers retain some ICL capabilities even when the label associations are obfuscated. We provide evidence that transformers can reason with and understand sequentiality encoded within function classes, as reflected by the effective learning of our proposed tasks. Our results also show that the performance deteriorated with increasing randomness in the labels, though not to the extent one might expect, implying a potential robustness of learned sequentiality against label noise. Future research may want to look into how previous explanations of transformers, such as induction heads and task vectors, relate to sequentiality in ICL in these toy examples. Our investigation lays the groundwork for further research into how transformers process and perceive sequential data.

papers.title: Too Much in Common: Shifting of Embeddings in Transformer Language Models and its Implications
papers.research_question: Why do embeddings in Transformer language models become anisotropic, and how can isotropy be restored to improve performance on semantic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that embeddings in Transformer language models drift in a common direction due to the common enemies effect, and that simply centering the embeddings restores isotropy and improves performance on semantic tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that embeddings drift in a shared direction and that centering is an effective method to restore isotropy and improve semantic performance.
papers.key_findings:
Embeddings in Transformer models drift in a common direction due to the common enemies effect, where non-target words receive gradients in the same direction.
Centering the embedding matrix (removing the mean) restores isotropy of the embeddings.
Centering improves performance on word similarity and relatedness tasks, especially for rare words.
future_direction: Investigating the dynamics of the interactions between representations and embeddings.
Improving embeddings of rare words.
Formulating more computationally efficient training objectives.
papers.abstract: The success of language models based on the Transformer architecture appears to be inconsistent with observed anisotropic properties of representations learned by such models. We resolve this by showing, contrary to previous studies, that the representations do not occupy a narrow cone, but rather drift in common directions. At any training step, all of the embeddings except for the ground-truth target embedding are updated with gradient in the same direction. Compounded over the training set, the embeddings drift and share common components, manifested in their shape in all the models we have empirically tested. Our experiments show that isotropy can be restored using a simple transformation. 1

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year.
