We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Characterizing Intrinsic Compositionality in Transformers with Tree Projections
papers.research_question: Does the transformer learn a tree-like computation when trained on language data, and how can we measure its tree-structuredness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised, parameter-free method to functionally project transformers into tree-structured networks, showing that transformers become more tree-like during training and that tree-structuredness predicts compositional generalization.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results suggest that making further progress on human-like compositional generalization might require inductive biases that encourage the emergence of latent tree-like structure.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers become more tree-like over training on sequence transduction tasks.
Tree projections sometimes align with gold syntax.
Induced trees reflect contextual dependence structure.
Tree-structuredness correlates better with compositional generalization than in-domain accuracy.
Self-supervised training does not lead to tree-like computation in low data regimes.
papers.abstract: When trained on language data, do transformers learn some arbitrary computation that utilizes the full capacity of the architecture or do they learn a simpler, tree-like computation, hypothesized to underlie compositional meaning systems like human languages? There is an apparent tension between compositional accounts of human language understanding, which are based on a restricted bottom-up computational process, and the enormous success of neural models like transformers, which can route information arbitrarily between different parts of their input. One possibility is that these models, while extremely flexible in principle, in practice learn to interpret language hierarchically, ultimately building sentence representations close to those predictable by a bottom-up, tree-structured model. To evaluate this possibility, we describe an unsupervised and parameter-free method to \emph{functionally project} the behavior of any transformer into the space of tree-structured networks. Given an input sentence, we produce a binary tree that approximates the transformer's representation-building process and a score that captures how "tree-like" the transformer's behavior is on the input. While calculation of this score does not require training any additional models, it provably upper-bounds the fit between a transformer and any tree-structured approximation. Using this method, we show that transformers for three different tasks become more tree-like over the course of training, in some cases unsupervisedly recovering the same trees as supervised parsers. These trees, in turn, are predictive of model behavior, with more tree-like models generalizing better on tests of compositional generalization.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: Extending a Mathematical Theory of the Emergence of Knowledge from the Experience to Capture Learning Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers' learning dynamics emerge from the structure of training data, and how does this relate to human semantic development?
papers.core_contribution: Extends a mathematical theory of learning dynamics to minimal transformers, demonstrating that learning trajectories are predictable from data structure and mirror human semantic development.
papers.conclusion: The work provides initial steps toward understanding how transformers learn, demonstrating that experience guides learning in a way that mirrors human semantic development, and the mathematical theory helps capture these dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Learning occurs in two phases: fast reduction of loss-between via relation information, and slower reduction of loss-within via item information through attention.
Learning dynamics follow sigmoidal trajectories for dataset dimensions, as predicted by deep linear network theory.
The model exhibits progressive differentiation of concepts, learning broader categories before finer ones.
The model shows U-shaped learning for certain features, such as overgeneralization of properties.
Embeddings from the minimal transformer correlate with those from larger LLMs, suggesting relevance to scaled-up models.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified toy dataset and minimal transformer architecture, which may not fully capture complexities of natural language and larger models.
future_direction: Extending models and training sets to more natural language datasets.
Exploring how attentional strategies emerge for handling longer contextual dependencies.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture used in LLMs has garnered widespread attention due to these model's human-like conceptual knowledge and language understanding, yet understanding how these models' capabilities result from experience-guided learning, and connecting this learning process with the structure in their training data, can seem intractable. Here we present preliminary steps to characterizing the developmental trajectory of a minimal Transformer trained on a next-token prediction task, using a simple dataset with quantifiable uncertainty and a simple, intuitively characterizable structure that captures some aspects of natural semantic structure learned by LLMs from large datasets. We show how the dynamic learning process of this model is a predictable consequence of the structure of the training data, exhibiting attested features of human semantic development, as captured in a theory of neural network learning dynamics (Saxe et. al. 2019) previously used to capture such dynamics in a network originally introduced by Rumelhart & Todd (1993).

papers.title: Position, Padding and Predictions: A Deeper Look at Position Information in CNNs
papers.research_question: How do CNNs encode absolute position information, and what is the role of padding and boundary effects in this encoding?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that zero padding in CNNs leads to encoding of absolute position information, which impacts boundary effects and can either help or hurt performance depending on the task.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that zero padding drives CNNs to encode absolute position information, which has significant implications for various vision tasks, both positive and negative.
papers.key_findings:
Zero padding encodes more absolute position information than other padding types (e.g., reflection, replicate, circular).
Position information is stored more in deeper layers of CNNs.
Black canvas (zeros) injects more position information than white or mean canvas.
Boundary effects affect all image regions, not just the border.
Position encoding can improve performance for tasks like segmentation but hurt for tasks requiring translation invariance like texture recognition.
papers.abstract: In contrast to fully connected networks, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) achieve efficiency by learning weights associated with local filters with a finite spatial extent. An implication of this is that a filter may know what it is looking at, but not where it is positioned in the image. In this paper, we first test this hypothesis and reveal that a surprising degree of absolute position information is encoded in commonly used CNNs. We show that zero padding drives CNNs to encode position information in their internal representations, while a lack of padding precludes position encoding. This gives rise to deeper questions about the role of position information in CNNs: (i) What boundary heuristics enable optimal position encoding for downstream tasks?; (ii) Does position encoding affect the learning of semantic representations?; (iii) Does position encoding always improve performance? To provide answers, we perform the largest case study to date on the role that padding and border heuristics play in CNNs. We design novel tasks which allow us to quantify boundary effects as a function of the distance to the border. Numerous semantic objectives reveal the effect of the border on semantic representations. Finally, we demonstrate the implications of these findings on multiple real-world tasks to show that position information can both help or hurt performance.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: Understanding the Expressive Power and Mechanisms of Transformer for Sequence Modeling
papers.research_question: What is the expressive power of Transformer for sequence modeling with long, sparse, and complicated memory, and what are the mechanisms of its components?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of the expressive power of Transformer for sequence modeling with long, sparse memories, establishing approximation rates and elucidating the distinct roles of components like attention heads, feed-forward layers, dot-product, and positional encoding.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical insights offer natural suggestions for alternative Transformer architectures and provide a framework for understanding their mechanisms in sequence modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Deeper Transformers are necessary for memories with intricate nested relationships, while for independent memories, a single layer with sufficient heads and width suffices.
Feed-forward layers approximate nonlinear memory and readout functions, while attention layers extract tokens from memory locations.
The dot-product in attention is not necessary for fixed memories but is essential for adaptive memories due to the needed nonlinearity and interaction with positional encoding.
Relative positional encoding with logarithmic decay (log-RPE) is more efficient for heavy-tailed memories, while linear decay (lin-RPE) is better for light-tailed memories.
Increasing the depth of the Transformer can mitigate the required number of attention heads and feed-forward width.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis focuses on specific types of memory (fixed, adaptive, essentially sparse) and uses synthetic data for experimental validation, which may not fully capture real-world complexities.
papers.abstract: We conduct a systematic study of the approximation properties of Transformer for sequence modeling with long, sparse and complicated memory. We investigate the mechanisms through which different components of Transformer, such as the dot-product self-attention, positional encoding and feed-forward layer, affect its expressive power, and we study their combined effects through establishing explicit approximation rates. Our study reveals the roles of critical parameters in the Transformer, such as the number of layers and the number of attention heads. These theoretical insights are validated experimentally and offer natural suggestions for alternative architectures.

papers.title: Beyond Semantics: How Temporal Biases Shape Retrieval in Transformer and State-Space Models
papers.research_question: How do temporal biases shape information retrieval in transformer and state-space models during in-context learning, and how effectively can these models differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that both transformer and state-space models exhibit strong temporal biases (primacy and recency effects) in retrieving information, and in transformers, these biases are mechanistically linked to the function of induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Temporal biases are fundamental to in-context learning in both transformer and state-space architectures, shaping information retrieval in ways analogous to human episodic memory, with induction heads playing a key mechanistic role in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Both transformer and state-space models show a tendency for serial recall, predicting the token immediately following a repeated instance ('+1' token).
The strength of serial recall is modulated by the token's temporal position, showing strong primacy and recency effects, with model-specific biases (e.g., Mistral shows recency, Falcon-Mamba shows primacy).
Ablating induction heads in transformers significantly impairs both serial recall and the ability to selectively retrieve correct episodes in the presence of interference, confirming their causal role.
Despite architectural differences, state-space models exhibit comparable temporal biases to transformers, suggesting these biases arise from fundamental properties of sequential data processing.
Episodic retrieval is less reliable for memories embedded in the middle of a prompt, demonstrating a 'lost in the middle' effect even when semantic content is neutralized.
papers.limitation: The study primarily uses token-random prompts rather than natural text and analyzes next-token probabilities, representing a simplified information environment that isolates temporal effects from semantic confounds.
future_direction: Future work can explore the more complex interplay between 'when' something was said and 'what' was said in rich, semantic contexts.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is governed by both temporal and semantic relationships, shaping how Large Language Models (LLMs) retrieve contextual information. Analogous to human episodic memory, where the retrieval of specific events is enabled by separating events that happened at different times, this work probes the ability of various pretrained LLMs, including transformer and state-space models, to differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events. Specifically, we prompted models with sequences containing multiple presentations of the same token, which reappears at the sequence end. By fixing the positions of these repeated tokens and permuting all others, we removed semantic confounds and isolated temporal effects on next-token prediction. Across diverse sequences, models consistently placed the highest probabilities on tokens following a repeated token, but with a notable bias for those nearest the beginning or end of the input. An ablation experiment linked this phenomenon in transformers to induction heads. Extending the analysis to unique semantic contexts with partial overlap further demonstrated that memories embedded in the middle of a prompt are retrieved less reliably. Despite architectural differences, state-space and transformer models showed comparable temporal biases. Our findings deepen the understanding of temporal biases in in-context learning and offer an illustration of how these biases can enable temporal separation and episodic retrieval.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformers Models
papers.research_question: How to interactively explore and understand what attention heads in transformer models have learned, specifically in BERT, by combining attention visualization with nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to explore and explain learned representations and attention mechanisms in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is an interactive visualization tool that uses linguistic annotations, interactive masking, and nearest neighbor search to reveal intelligible structure in learned representations of transformer models, demonstrated with BERT on the Wizard of Oz corpus.
papers.key_findings:
At early layers (e.g., layer 1), masked token embeddings show similarity to common tokens like punctuation and determinants, with no meaningful linguistic information encoded.
As layers progress, more part-of-speech information is added; by layer 6, BERT becomes confident that a masked token is a verb, refining this estimation in later layers.
Complex dependencies such as direct object (DOBJ) are detected in early-middle layers but rely on a combination of multiple attention heads, not individual heads.
Positional heads attend to succeeding or preceding tokens and encode linguistic information about the attended-to word, such as part-of-speech and dependency relations.
EXBERT enables interactive exploration of how attention heads contribute to encoding linguistic features in token embeddings through nearest neighbor search on annotated corpora.
papers.abstract: Large language models can produce powerful contextual representations that lead to improvements across many NLP tasks. Since these models are typically guided by a sequence of learned self attention mechanisms and may comprise undesired inductive biases, it is paramount to be able to explore what the attention has learned. While static analyses of these models lead to targeted insights, interactive tools are more dynamic and can help humans better gain an intuition for the model-internal reasoning process. We present exBERT, an interactive tool named after the popular BERT language model, that provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations by matching a human-specified input to similar contexts in a large annotated dataset. By aggregating the annotations of the matching similar contexts, exBERT helps intuitively explain what each attention-head has learned.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: What Do Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn?
papers.research_question: What do self-supervised vision transformers learn? Specifically, how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and downstream task performance.
papers.core_contribution: CL and MIM learn complementary representations: CL captures global shape information but suffers from attention collapse, while MIM captures local texture information and preserves diversity. A simple linear combination of both losses can outperform each individually.
papers.conclusion: CL and MIM have opposing properties and are complementary; combining them can improve performance, and even a simple harmonization method shows benefits.
papers.key_findings:
CL trains self-attentions to capture global patterns and object shapes, but leads to attention collapse into homogeneity, reducing representation diversity.
MIM focuses on local patterns and textures, preserving token-level diversity and excelling in fine-tuning and dense prediction tasks.
CL utilizes low-frequency signals (shape-biased), while MIM utilizes high-frequency signals (texture-biased).
CL plays a crucial role in later layers, while MIM is important in early layers.
A simple linear combination of CL and MIM objectives can leverage the advantages of both methods, improving performance in linear probing and fine-tuning.
future_direction: Exploring better ways to combine CL and MIM than linear combination, such as applying CL in later layers and MIM in early layers.
Extending findings to multi-stage Vision Transformers like PiT and Swin.
Enhancing individual properties of CL and MIM to improve shape or texture learning.
papers.abstract: We present a comparative study on how and why contrastive learning (CL) and masked image modeling (MIM) differ in their representations and in their performance of downstream tasks. In particular, we demonstrate that self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) have the following properties: (1) CL trains self-attentions to capture longer-range global patterns than MIM, such as the shape of an object, especially in the later layers of the ViT architecture. This CL property helps ViTs linearly separate images in their representation spaces. However, it also makes the self-attentions collapse into homogeneity for all query tokens and heads. Such homogeneity of self-attention reduces the diversity of representations, worsening scalability and dense prediction performance. (2) CL utilizes the low-frequency signals of the representations, but MIM utilizes high-frequencies. Since low- and high-frequency information respectively represent shapes and textures, CL is more shape-oriented and MIM more texture-oriented. (3) CL plays a crucial role in the later layers, while MIM mainly focuses on the early layers. Upon these analyses, we find that CL and MIM can complement each other and observe that even the simplest harmonization can help leverage the advantages of both methods. The code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/cl-vs-mim.

papers.title: Visualizing LLM Latent Space Geometry Through Dimensionality Reduction
papers.research_question: How does the internal geometric structure of latent states in Transformer-based language models evolve across layers and components?
papers.core_contribution: This paper visualizes and analyzes the latent space geometry of Transformer-based LLMs, revealing a clear geometric separation between attention and MLP component outputs, characterizing high-norm latent states at initial sequence positions, and visualizing layerwise evolution and positional effects.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how dimensionality reduction can reveal geometric patterns in LLM latent spaces, contributing to interpretability research and motivating further analysis of feature geometry across models and conditions.
papers.key_findings:
A clear geometric separation exists between the outputs of attention and MLP components in intermediate layers, a pattern not previously documented.
Latent states at the initial sequence position have high norms, extending beyond special tokens in LLaMa despite its use of relative positional encodings.
Layerwise norms of latent states (excluding initial tokens) gradually increase and then spike in the final block before dropping after the final normalization.
GPT-2's learned positional embeddings form a high-dimensional helical structure in latent space.
LLaMa's sequence-position-dependent latent states show a low-dimensional geometric pattern, though the cause (RoPE vs. other factors) remains unclear.
papers.limitation: For LLaMa, the visualizations alone cannot determine whether the observed geometric patterns are due to RoPE, the convergence of features from self-attention heads, or both.
future_direction: Further understanding the dynamics of latent states across layers, models, and experimental conditions.
Interpreting the sequence-wise latent state geometric patterns of models using Rotary Positional Encodings (RoPE).
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve state-of-the-art results across many natural language tasks, but their internal mechanisms remain difficult to interpret. In this work, we extract, process, and visualize latent state geometries in Transformer-based language models through dimensionality reduction. We capture layerwise activations at multiple points within Transformer blocks and enable systematic analysis through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP). We demonstrate experiments on GPT-2 and LLaMa models, where we uncover interesting geometric patterns in latent space. Notably, we identify a clear separation between attention and MLP component outputs across intermediate layers, a pattern not documented in prior work to our knowledge. We also characterize the high norm of latent states at the initial sequence position and visualize the layerwise evolution of latent states. Additionally, we demonstrate the high-dimensional helical structure of GPT-2's positional embeddings and the sequence-wise geometric patterns in LLaMa. We make our code available at https://github.com/Vainateya/Feature_Geometry_Visualization.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers.research_question: Why do heuristics such as cosine annealing (SGDR), learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation improve the convergence and performance of deep learning models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA) to empirically investigate the reasons behind the success of deep learning heuristics like cosine annealing, learning rate warmup, and knowledge distillation.
papers.conclusion: The empirical analysis using mode connectivity and CCA sheds light on the heuristics of cosine annealing, warmup, and distillation, suggesting that common explanations are oversimplified and opening new questions for deeper exploration.
papers.key_findings:
The reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing (e.g., escaping local minima) are not evidenced in practice; iterates move over barriers after restarts but this is an oversimplification.
The effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers (e.g., fully-connected stack) from creating training instability; freezing these layers achieves similar outcomes.
In knowledge distillation, the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers of the student network.
Mode connectivity is a robust framework for connecting optima obtained from vastly different training schemes (e.g., different optimizers, batch sizes, regularization).
For SGDR, the path found by mode connectivity corresponds to lower training loss but higher validation loss than the iterates, suggesting a generalization gap.
papers.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
papers.research_question: What is the function of feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models? The paper shows they operate as key-value memories.
papers.core_contribution: Feed-forward layers in transformer language models function as key-value memories, where keys capture input patterns and values represent output distributions, and the model's final output is constructed by composing and refining these memories across layers.
papers.conclusion: Feed-forward layers in transformers act as pattern-detecting key-value memories, and the model's output is gradually constructed by composing these memories within layers and refining them across layers via residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Keys in feed-forward layers correlate with human-interpretable input patterns, with lower layers capturing shallow patterns (e.g., n-grams) and upper layers capturing semantic patterns.
Values in upper layers induce distributions over the output vocabulary that correlate with the next-token distribution of the patterns in the corresponding keys.
The output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of hundreds of active memories, rarely dominated by a single memory cell.
Residual connections act as a refinement mechanism, with the feed-forward layer often vetoing the residual's top prediction to shift probability mass to other candidates.
The model's final prediction is often determined in the lower layers, with upper layers refining the confidence and occasionally changing the prediction.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to one language model and dataset, and the assumption that all layers operate in the same embedding space may not hold for lower layers.
future_direction: Investigating the transformation of embedding spaces across layers and the interplay between feed-forward and self-attention layers.
Extending the analysis to other transformer models, such as BERT encoders and neural translation models.
Exploring practical implications for interpretability methods, data privacy (e.g., membership inference), and architectural innovations.
papers.abstract: Feed-forward layers constitute two-thirds of a transformer model's parameters, yet their role in the network remains under-explored. We show that feed-forward layers in transformerbased language models operate as key-value memories, where each key correlates with textual patterns in the training examples, and each value induces a distribution over the output vocabulary. Our experiments show that the learned patterns are human-interpretable, and that lower layers tend to capture shallow patterns, while upper layers learn more semantic ones. The values complement the keys' input patterns by inducing output distributions that concentrate probability mass on tokens likely to appear immediately after each pattern, particularly in the upper layers. Finally, we demonstrate that the output of a feed-forward layer is a composition of its memories, which is subsequently refined throughout the model's layers via residual connections to produce the final output distribution.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: A Primer on the Inner Workings of Transformer-based Language Models
papers.core_contribution: Provides a concise technical introduction to interpretability techniques for Transformer-based language models and a comprehensive overview of known internal mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: The primer consolidates current interpretability techniques and known mechanisms, providing a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Summarizes known internal mechanisms of Transformer LMs, such as attention patterns and feedforward network functions.
Highlights the residual stream as a key perspective for understanding model computations.
Surveys techniques for behavior localization (e.g., logit attribution, causal interventions) and information decoding (e.g., probing, sparse autoencoders).
papers.abstract: The rapid progress of research aimed at interpreting the inner workings of advanced language models has highlighted a need for contextualizing the insights gained from years of work in this area. This primer provides a concise technical introduction to the current techniques used to interpret the inner workings of Transformer-based language models, focusing on the generative decoder-only architecture. We conclude by presenting a comprehensive overview of the known internal mechanisms implemented by these models, uncovering connections across popular approaches and active research directions in this area.

papers.title: Jump to Conclusions: Short-Cutting Transformers With Linear Transformations
papers.research_question: Is there a more accurate way to cast hidden representations into final representation substitutes than interpreting them as they are (identity mapping)?
papers.core_contribution: A simple method using linear transformations to cast hidden representations to final-layer substitutes, which improves interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Linear mappings provide a simple and effective way to enhance the utilization of hidden representations for interpretability and efficiency, revealing linear structure in transformer components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear mappings (mat) consistently outperform identity mapping (id) in approximating future hidden representations and final predictions.
The method allows accurate prediction estimation from early layers, showing that models often predict the final output early.
The learned linear mappings generalize well across different model scales and data distributions.
When applied to early exiting, the method saves additional layers (e.g., 7.9% for GPT-2, 5.4% for BERT) while retaining 95% accuracy.
Attention sub-modules are the most tolerant to linear approximation compared to FFN and layer normalization.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on linear transformations, leaving affine or non-linear transformations for future work.
Does not elucidate the reason for the linear structure observed in transformer inference.
Only considers post-hoc interpretability (analyzing trained models without changing weights).
Experiments are conducted only on English data.
future_direction: Exploring affine or non-linear transformations for casting hidden representations.
Integrating linear mappings into model training rather than only post-hoc analysis.
Breaking the computation into parallel tasks to improve efficiency.
Comparing the method with other approaches like Belrose et al. (2023).
Investigating the reasons for the linear structure in transformer components.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models create hidden representations of their inputs at every layer, but only use final-layer representations for prediction. This obscures the internal decision-making process of the model and the utility of its intermediate representations. One way to elucidate this is to cast the hidden representations as final representations, bypassing the transformer computation in-between. In this work, we suggest a simple method for such casting, using linear transformations. This approximation far exceeds the prevailing practice of inspecting hidden representations from all layers, in the space of the final layer. Moreover, in the context of language modeling, our method produces more accurate predictions from hidden layers, across various model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This allows "peeking" into intermediate representations, showing that GPT-2 and BERT often predict the final output already in early layers. We then demonstrate the practicality of our method to recent early exit strategies, showing that when aiming, for example, at retention of 95% accuracy, our approach saves additional 7.9% layers for GPT-2 and 5.4% layers for BERT. Last, we extend our method to linearly approximate sub-modules, finding that attention is most tolerant to this change. Our code and learned mappings are publicly available at https://github.com/sashayd/mat.

papers.title: Retrieval-Aware Distillation for Transformer-SSM Hybrids
papers.research_question: How can we bridge the performance gap between Transformers and State-Space Models (SSMs) on tasks requiring in-context retrieval by preserving only retrieval-critical attention heads during distillation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces retrieval-aware distillation, a method that preserves only retrieval-critical attention heads when distilling a Transformer into a Transformer-SSM hybrid, achieving comparable performance with far fewer attention heads and significantly reduced memory overhead.
papers.conclusion: Retrieval-aware distillation enables efficient Transformer-SSM hybrids by preserving only retrieval-critical attention heads, closing the performance gap with Transformers at a fraction of the memory cost.
papers.key_findings:
Retaining just 2% of attention heads (10 heads in a 1B model) recovers over 95% of teacher performance on retrieval-heavy tasks.
Retrieval-aware distillation reduces memory usage by 5-6x compared to heuristic hybrid baselines.
Once retrieval is handled by a few attention heads, the SSM backbone can be simplified (e.g., 8x reduction in state dimension) with limited performance loss.
The retrieval functionality remains localized in the preserved attention heads after distillation.
The method outperforms heuristic attention placement strategies that require 10x more attention heads.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on models below 3B parameters, so scalability is unclear.
Head selection relies on a synthetic KV-retrieval probe that may not capture all retrieval settings (e.g., multi-hop retrieval).
Does not enforce KV sharing across layers, which could further reduce memory.
Retrieval is not fully separated from the recurrent backbone; some SSM heads still affect retrieval tasks, limiting how aggressively the state dimension can be reduced.
future_direction: Investigating whether the same small set of heads remains sufficient at larger scale.
Extending the retrieval probe to capture other retrieval settings.
Enabling KV sharing during distillation to further reduce the KV cache.
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) offer efficient sequence modeling but lag behind Transformers on benchmarks that require in-context retrieval. Prior work links this gap to a small set of attention heads, termed Gather-and-Aggregate (G&A), which SSMs struggle to reproduce. We propose *retrieval-aware distillation*, which converts a pretrained Transformer into a hybrid student by preserving only these retrieval-critical heads and distilling the rest into recurrent heads. We identify the essential heads via ablation on a synthetic retrieval task, producing a hybrid with sparse, non-uniform attention placement. We show that preserving **just 2% of attention heads recovers over 95% of teacher performance on retrieval-heavy tasks** (10 heads in a 1B model), requiring far fewer heads than hybrids that retain at least 25%. We further find that large recurrent states often compensate for missing retrieval: once retrieval is handled by these heads, the SSM backbone can be simplified with limited loss, even with an $8\times$ reduction in state dimension. By reducing both the attention cache and the SSM state, the resulting hybrid is $5$--$6\times$ more memory-efficient than comparable hybrids, closing the Transformer--SSM gap at a fraction of the memory cost.

papers.title: Looking Beyond The Top-1: Transformers Determine Top Tokens In Order
papers.research_question: What computation is the Transformer model performing after the saturation event (where the top-1 prediction becomes fixed)?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers determine their top-k output tokens in order of ranking via a discrete task-transition mechanism, a phenomenon intrinsic to the architecture that can be leveraged for improved early-exit strategies and language modeling.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Transformer layers after the top-1 saturation event work on determining lower-ranked tokens in order, proposes a task-transition mechanism underlying this, and shows practical benefits for efficiency and accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Top-k tokens in Transformers reach saturation (become fixed) sequentially in the order of their final ranking.
This ordered saturation occurs across text, vision, and speech modalities and in untrained models, suggesting it is architecture-inherent.
A simple classifier can predict the current 'task' (which token rank is being determined) from hidden layer embeddings.
Intervening by injecting activations from a saturation layer can causally trigger a transition to the next task.
A novel early-exit strategy based on task transition outperforms existing token-level confidence measures.
papers.limitation:
The analysis does not determine which specific components in the Transformer architecture give rise to the ordered saturation phenomenon.
The work does not consider whether the data used was encountered during the models' training.
future_direction: Ablation studies to identify which Transformer components are responsible for the ordered saturation.
Investigating if other DNN architectures (e.g., RNNs) also determine top-k tokens in order.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of Transformers is crucial for achieving more accurate and efficient predictions. In this work, we analyze the computation performed by Transformers in the layers after the top-1 prediction has become fixed, which has been previously referred to as the "saturation event". We expand the concept of saturation events for top-k tokens, demonstrating that similar saturation events occur across language, vision, and speech models. We find that these saturation events happen in order of the corresponding tokens' ranking, i.e., the model first decides on the top ranking token, then the second highest ranking token, and so on. This phenomenon seems intrinsic to the Transformer architecture, occurring across different architectural variants (decoder-only, encoder-only, and to a lesser extent full-Transformer), and even in untrained Transformers. We propose an underlying mechanism of task transition for this sequential saturation, where task k corresponds to predicting the k-th most probable token, and the saturation events are in fact discrete transitions between the tasks. In support of this we show that it is possible to predict the current task from hidden layer embedding. Furthermore, using an intervention method we demonstrate that we can cause the model to switch from one task to the next. Finally, leveraging our findings, we introduce a novel token-level early-exit strategy, which surpasses existing methods in balancing performance and efficiency.

papers.title: Why transformers are obviously good models of language
papers.research_question: Why are transformers effective models of language, and how do they align with theoretical perspectives on language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers are good models of language because their architecture, such as word embeddings and attention mechanisms, aligns with cognitive linguistic theories like prototype theory and construction grammar.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are effective models of language, and their alignment with certain linguistic theories suggests that these theories, such as those from cognitive linguistics, are correct.
papers.key_findings:
Word embeddings in transformers represent prototypical meanings of words, similar to Rosch's prototype theory.
Contextualized word meanings are constructed through self-attention layers, updating prototypes based on context.
Transformers can handle syntax and top-down processing via attention heads and skip connections, analogous to construction grammar.
Transformers lack a bias for local dependencies, allowing them to learn rare long-distance dependencies effectively.
The empirical success of transformers supports cognitive linguistic approaches over traditional syntactic theories.
papers.limitation:
Transformers assert false facts with the same degree of authority as true information.
Transformers have myopia in social contexts, such as not remembering past interactions in chatbots.
papers.abstract: Nobody knows how language works, but many theories abound. Transformers are a class of neural networks that process language automatically with more success than alternatives, both those based on neural computations and those that rely on other (e.g. more symbolic) mechanisms. Here, I highlight direct connections between the transformer architecture and certain theoretical perspectives on language. The empirical success of transformers relative to alternative models provides circumstantial evidence that the linguistic approaches that transformers embody should be, at least, evaluated with greater scrutiny by the linguistics community and, at best, considered to be the currently best available theories.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Interpret the Predictions of Deep Networks via Re-Label Distillation
papers.research_question: How to interpret the predictions of deep neural networks by learning a direct map from input to prediction via re-label distillation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a re-label distillation approach that uses synthetic images generated by a VAE and knowledge distillation to train a linear model for interpreting predictions of deep networks.
papers.conclusion: The re-label distillation approach effectively interprets predictions of deep networks and provides research ideas for explainable AI.
papers.key_findings:
The re-label distillation approach generates saliency maps that accurately mark important features for predictions.
It outperforms state-of-the-art methods on deletion and insertion metrics for interpretability.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the predictions of a black-box deep network can facilitate the reliability of its deployment. In this work, we propose a re-label distillation approach to learn a direct map from the input to the prediction in a self-supervision manner. The image is projected into a VAE subspace to generate some synthetic images by randomly perturbing its latent vector. Then, these synthetic images can be annotated into one of two classes by identifying whether their labels shift. After that, using the labels annotated by the deep network as teacher, a linear student model is trained to approximate the annotations by mapping these synthetic images to the classes. In this manner, these re-labeled synthetic images can well describe the local classification mechanism of the deep network, and the learned student can provide a more intuitive explanation towards the predictions. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of our approach qualitatively and quantitatively.

papers.title: Learning a Fourier Transform for Linear Relative Positional Encodings in Transformers
papers.research_question: How to efficiently incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs) into linear Transformers, enabling linear complexity for both sequential and geometric data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), a class of linear Transformers that efficiently incorporate relative positional encodings (RPEs) by learning their spectral representation, achieving linear complexity and applicability to sequential and geometric data.
papers.conclusion: FLTs provide an efficient and effective method for incorporating RPEs into linear attention Transformers, with theoretical approximation guarantees and strong empirical performance across text, image, and 3D molecular data.
papers.key_findings:
FLTs outperform other linear Transformers (e.g., Performer, CosFormer) on language modeling (WikiText-103) by achieving lower perplexity.
FLTs achieve higher accuracy than baselines on image classification tasks (ImageNet, Places365, Fashion-MNIST).
For 3D molecular property prediction (OC20 dataset), FLTs with RPEs provide better energy prediction accuracy (lower MAE, higher EwT) than Performers without RPEs.
FLTs maintain linear time and space complexity, being more memory-efficient than log-linear Performer baselines.
FLTs can learn local RPEs and exhibit both local and global attention patterns in language modeling.
papers.abstract: We propose a new class of linear Transformers called FourierLearner-Transformers (FLTs), which incorporate a wide range of relative positional encoding mechanisms (RPEs). These include regular RPE techniques applied for sequential data, as well as novel RPEs operating on geometric data embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. FLTs construct the optimal RPE mechanism implicitly by learning its spectral representation. As opposed to other architectures combining efficient low-rank linear attention with RPEs, FLTs remain practical in terms of their memory usage and do not require additional assumptions about the structure of the RPE mask. Besides, FLTs allow for applying certain structural inductive bias techniques to specify masking strategies, e.g. they provide a way to learn the so-called local RPEs introduced in this paper and give accuracy gains as compared with several other linear Transformers for language modeling. We also thoroughly test FLTs on other data modalities and tasks, such as image classification, 3D molecular modeling, and learnable optimizers. To the best of our knowledge, for 3D molecular data, FLTs are the first Transformer architectures providing linear attention and incorporating RPE masking.

papers.title: From Low-Rank Features to Encoding Mismatch: Rethinking Feature Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-map knowledge distillation (KD), which works so well for CNNs, usually fail for Vision Transformers (ViTs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students in Vision Transformers as the reason for the failure of feature-map knowledge distillation, and proposes two minimal strategies (post-hoc feature lifting and native width alignment) to resolve this mismatch, reactivating simple feature distillation.
papers.conclusion: The encoding mismatch is the key reason for the failure of feature distillation in ViTs, and the proposed strategies effectively resolve this mismatch, providing a simple and interpretable design cue for compact ViT architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT representations are globally low-rank, with a small number of singular components capturing most of the feature energy.
Despite global low-rank structure, individual tokens use a high fraction of channel capacity, leading to an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students.
This encoding mismatch explains why naive feature-map distillation fails in ViTs.
Two proposed strategies (post-hoc feature lifting and native width alignment) reactivate feature distillation, improving DeiT-Tiny accuracy by up to 3.37% when distilling from CaiT-S24.
The architectural modifications also improve standalone student performance without distillation, indicating a genuine bottleneck in compact ViTs.
papers.abstract: Feature-map knowledge distillation (KD) is highly effective for convolutional networks but often fails for Vision Transformers (ViTs). To understand this failure and guide method design, we conduct a two-view representation analysis of ViTs. First, a layer-wise Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of full feature matrices shows that final-layer representations are globally low-rank: for CaiT-S24, only $121/61/34/14$ dimensions suffice to capture $99\%/95\%/90\%/80\%$ of the energy. In principle, this suggests that a compact student plus a simple linear projector should be enough for feature alignment, contradicting the weak empirical performance of standard feature KD. To resolve this paradox, we introduce a token-level Spectral Energy Pattern (SEP) analysis that measures how each token uses channel capacity. SEP reveals that, despite the global low-rank structure, individual tokens distribute energy over most channels, forming a high-bandwidth encoding pattern. This results in an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students. Motivated by this insight, we propose two minimal, mismatch-driven strategies: (1) post-hoc feature lifting with a lightweight projector retained during inference, or (2) native width alignment that widens only the student's last block to the teacher's width. On ImageNet-1K, these strategies reactivate simple feature-map distillation in ViTs, raising DeiT-Tiny accuracy from $74.86\%$ to $77.53\%$ and $78.23\%$ when distilling from CaiT-S24, while also improving standalone students trained without any teacher. Our analysis thus explains why ViT feature distillation fails and shows how exploiting low-rank structure yields effective, interpretable remedies and concrete design guidance for compact ViTs.

papers.title: Beyond Position: the emergence of wavelet-like properties in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models with Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) develop emergent, wavelet-like properties to compensate for the positional encoding's theoretical limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models with RoPE overcome the theoretical limitations of their positional encoding by spontaneously developing emergent, wavelet-like multi-resolution processing strategies in their attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models equipped with RoPE actively overcome their theoretical limitations by developing emergent, wavelet-like processing strategies, which represent a fundamental and multi-faceted characteristic of modern language models.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in RoPE-based models specialize into distinct frequency bands, forming a multi-resolution framework analogous to a wavelet transform.
This wavelet-like behavior is unique to RoPE compared to other positional encoding schemes like T5, BERT, or no encoding.
The development of these properties follows distinct evolutionary phases during training, including an exploratory phase and a specialization phase.
Models learn to respect the Heisenberg-Gabor uncertainty principle, exhibiting a negative trade-off between positional precision and spectral organization.
The wavelet-like organization provides scale-invariant representations, with robustness to changes in input sequence length.
papers.limitation:
The primary analysis examines model properties at inference time after training is complete; a more fine-grained, continuous analysis of training dynamics is needed.
Findings are based on a specific set of open-source language models trained predominantly on English text; generalization to other modalities, data types, and proprietary architectures requires further research.
future_direction: Fine-grained, continuous analysis of how spectral properties evolve during the training process.
Determining if these principles generalize across other modalities (e.g., vision, audio), data types (e.g., code, multilingual text), and proprietary architectures.
Using the wavelet framework as a new lens for interpretability and a benchmark for future positional encoding designs.
papers.abstract: This paper studies how Transformer models with Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) develop emergent, wavelet-like properties that compensate for the positional encoding's theoretical limitations. Through an analysis spanning model scales, architectures, and training checkpoints, we show that attention heads evolve to implement multi-resolution processing analogous to wavelet transforms. We demonstrate that this scale-invariant behavior is unique to RoPE, emerges through distinct evolutionary phases during training, and statistically adheres to the fundamental uncertainty principle. Our findings suggest that the effectiveness of modern Transformers stems from their remarkable ability to spontaneously develop optimal, multi-resolution decompositions to address inherent architectural constraints.

papers.title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Interpretable Policy Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide human-understandable explanations for deep reinforcement learning policies via interpretable policy distillation while maintaining high fidelity and performance?
papers.core_contribution: A unified framework for explainable reinforcement learning via interpretable policy distillation that achieves high fidelity, competitive performance, and both global and local explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework enables trustworthy deployment of RL agents in safety-critical applications by providing interpretable policies with high fidelity and performance.
papers.key_findings:
Distilled interpretable policies achieve high fidelity with minimal performance loss compared to teacher deep RL policies.
Ablation studies show that tree depth, loss function, and dataset size significantly impact fidelity and transparency.
Decision trees provide global explanations via the full tree structure and local explanations via path tracing for specific states.
papers.limitation:
Scaling to high-dimensional and visual inputs
Continuous control requires extensions of trees or sparse models
Online or incremental distillation for data efficiency
Human evaluation of explanations
Robustness under distribution shifts or rare states
Exploring interpretable frameworks beyond trees and linear policies
future_direction: Scaling to high-dimensional and visual inputs
Continuous control extensions
Online or incremental distillation for data efficiency
papers.abstract: Abstract—Deep reinforcement learning achieves remarkable performance but often operates as a black box, limiting trust in safety-critical applications. Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) aims to provide human-understandable explanations. We propose a unified framework for XRL via interpretable policy distillation, where a high-performing teacher policy is distilled into interpretable models such as decision trees or sparse linear policies. The distilled policy enables both global and local expla- nations while maintaining high fidelity. We provide theoretical guarantees on fidelity and performance, and perform extensive experiments with ablation studies. Results show that interpretable policies achieve competitive performance with high transparency, enabling deployment in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Directional Optimization Asymmetry in Transformers: A Synthetic Stress Test
papers.research_question: Do directional failures (like the reversal curse) in Transformers stem from linguistic statistics or from the architecture itself?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic, entropy-controlled benchmark to isolate directional optimization asymmetry in Transformers, showing that a directional gap persists even without linguistic priors, which is not present in MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The benchmark reveals a minimal, semantics-free signature of directional friction intrinsic to causal Transformer training, which persists even in a controlled synthetic environment.
papers.key_findings:
Scratch-trained Transformers exhibit a robust directional gap, with higher excess loss for inverse tasks compared to forward tasks, even in a symmetric data distribution.
MLPs show a much smaller directional gap, indicating that the asymmetry is specific to causal Transformer architecture.
Pre-trained Transformers show altered optimization dynamics, with increased forward excess loss but reduced inverse excess loss, resulting in a modest directional gap.
LoRA adaptation struggles with high-entropy inverse mappings due to capacity limitations, failing to match full fine-tuning performance.
The directional gap persists even when linguistic priors, token frequencies, and corpus-level asymmetries are removed, indicating an architectural bias.
papers.limitation:
The benchmark uses synthetic data with no semantic, grammatical, or hierarchical structure, limiting extrapolation to natural language tasks.
Experiments are limited to GPT-2 Small scale; larger models may exhibit different behavior.
Tokenizer mismatch: using a BPE tokenizer trained on English text on random character sequences may affect comparability.
Training configuration is fixed; alternative hyperparameters might shift results.
papers.abstract: Transformers are theoretically reversal-invariant: their function class does not prefer left-to-right over right-to-left mappings. Yet empirical studies on natural language repeatedly report a "reversal curse," and recent work on temporal asymmetry in LLMs suggests that real-world corpora carry their own arrow of time. This leaves an unresolved question: do directional failures stem from linguistic statistics, or from the architecture itself? We cut through this ambiguity with a fully synthetic, entropy-controlled benchmark designed as a clean-room stress test for directional learning. Using random string mappings with tunable branching factor K, we construct forward tasks with zero conditional entropy and inverse tasks with analytically determined entropy floors. Excess loss above these floors reveals that even scratch-trained GPT-2 models exhibit a strong, reproducible directional optimization gap (e.g., 1.16 nats at K=5), far larger than that of an MLP trained on the same data. Pre-trained initializations shift optimization behavior but do not eliminate this gap, while LoRA encounters a sharp capacity wall on high-entropy inverse mappings. Together, these results isolate a minimal, semantics-free signature of directional friction intrinsic to causal Transformer training-one that persists even when linguistic priors, token frequencies, and corpus-level temporal asymmetries are removed. Our benchmark provides a controlled instrument for dissecting directional biases in modern sequence models and motivates deeper mechanistic study of why inversion remains fundamentally harder for Transformers.

papers.title: How transformers learn structured data: insights from hierarchical filtering
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn structured data and approximate exact inference algorithms like Belief Propagation?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can approximate the exact inference algorithm (Belief Propagation) when trained on structured data, learning hierarchical correlations sequentially and implementing the algorithm in their attention maps.
papers.conclusion: The hierarchical filtering model provides insights into how transformers learn structured data, sequentially implementing longer-range correlations and approximating exact inference algorithms, with potential implications for curriculum learning and other domains.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve optimal performance on root classification and masked language modeling tasks, matching the Belief Propagation oracle.
Transformers output calibrated probabilities that approximate the exact marginals, even on out-of-sample data.
During training, transformers sequentially discover higher hierarchical correlation levels, aligning with partial inference algorithms.
Attention maps of trained transformers exhibit a structure that mirrors the generative tree and the Belief Propagation algorithm.
Probing experiments show that ancestor information is distributed across encoder layers, supporting sequential processing.
papers.limitation:
